Speakers and Main Topics Below is a list of speakers and topics presented at the event:
Speaker Organization / Role Topic Kiet Lam Senior Developer Engineer, FPT Software Development Application with AWS Serverless Kiet Nguyen & Viet Ly Software Engineer (VPBank), DevOps (VPBank) Optimizing Database Cost & Performance with Data Archiving Strategies Long Huynh Senior Solutions Architect, eCloudvalley Diffusion and OCR Vi Tran CloudOps Engineer, VIB Agentic AIOps on AWS: Inside AWS DevOps Agent Ngoc Tran Service Delivery Engineer Intern, Accenture From Local to Global: Migrating a GenAI Product to AWS Xuan Le & Nghi Danh Data Analytics & Insights, AI Engineer (Renova Cloud) Agentic Decision Intelligence on AWS Bao Huynh Cloud Native Developer, Endava Viet Nam AWS Principles Beyond AWS: How AWS Knowledge Transfers to Cloud-Native Roles Main Content On the morning of August 22, 2026, I attended FCAJ Community Day August at Bitexco Financial Tower. The event focused on AWS, Serverless, database optimization, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Cloud Operations. Here’s what I learned from the sessions:
1. Development Application with AWS Serverless This session introduced Serverless Computing and compared traditional application development with Serverless. The demo showed practical AWS Serverless application patterns.
Key points:
Serverless doesn’t mean no servers, but rather developers don’t need to manage servers. Benefits include automatic scaling and pay-per-use. Trade-offs to consider: cold start, execution time limits, stateless design. Connection to Fitness Assistant:
Serverless gives me another perspective on how certain workloads can be separated from continuously running backends. For example, event-driven tasks (sending notifications, image processing, nutrition calculations) or scheduled tasks (daily statistics aggregation) could consider using AWS Lambda instead of running services 24/7.
2. Optimizing Database Cost & Performance with Data Archiving Strategies This session dived deep into database growth and operational challenges as data increases. Content included data archiving architecture, initial data load design, daily incremental archiving, and cost optimization techniques.
Key points:
Not all data needs high-performance access. Data lifecycle and retention policy should be designed from the start. Cost optimization by separating hot data and cold data. Connection to Fitness Assistant:
The Fitness Assistant project can generate significant data over time such as weight history, InBody measurements, workout logs, nutrition logs, and activity history. From this session, I understand that as data volume increases, we shouldn’t just think about scaling the current database but also consider:
Which data needs frequent access (recent workouts, current stats) Which data can be archived (historical data from 1-2 years ago) Retention policy and storage cost Query performance optimization This is a direction that needs further research as the system grows.
3. Diffusion and OCR Session on AWS services for Text-to-Image generation and Image-to-Text extraction. The demo showed real-world use cases in image processing and analysis.
Key points:
Amazon Textract for OCR. Amazon Rekognition for image analysis. Integration with other AI services. Connection to Fitness Assistant:
This session helps me think more about future AI capabilities for Fitness Assistant. For example, OCR could be useful when users photograph nutrition labels to automatically extract nutritional information, or analyze images to assess posture during workouts. However, this is a future expansion direction; the project doesn’t currently have this functionality.
4. Agentic AIOps on AWS: Inside AWS DevOps Agent This was one of the most important sessions for my internship process. Content included AWS DevOps Agent, operational challenges, incident troubleshooting, investigation workflow, architecture overview, and security boundaries.
Key points:
Agent automatically analyzes logs and metrics to create hypotheses. Collects evidence from multiple sources (CloudWatch, X-Ray, logs). Provides recommendations based on context. Security boundaries and controlled automation. MCP (Model Context Protocol) extensibility. Direct connection to Fitness Assistant:
When deploying a system with multiple services like Fitness Assistant, we don’t just care about whether the application runs but also need to consider:
Monitoring: which service is having issues? Logs: where in the flow do errors occur? Incident investigation: why can’t service A connect to service B? Root cause analysis: is the problem network, security group, or application logic? Security boundary: ensure automated actions don’t cause risks. Observability: is there enough information to troubleshoot? This session directly relates to what I’m learning about Amazon CloudWatch and monitoring during my internship. I realize that a good production system needs the ability to self-observe and effectively support troubleshooting.
5. From Local to Global: Migrating a GenAI Product to AWS This session is particularly relevant to Fitness Assistant because the project has an AI service. Content included challenges when migrating GenAI product, moving from Azure OpenAI to Amazon Bedrock, Agentic AI systems, guardrails, evaluation frameworks, and operational governance.
Key points:
An AI production system is more than just calling a model API. Need guardrails to control output. Evaluation framework to assess quality. Operational governance for security and compliance. Migration considerations regarding cost, latency, model availability. Connection to Fitness Assistant:
This is especially meaningful because the project has an ai-service. The session helps me understand that when bringing AI workload to AWS, we need to consider:
Model integration architecture Security and data privacy Guardrails to ensure appropriate AI responses Evaluation to ensure quality Monitoring AI performance Governance and compliance Scalability and operational cost The session gives me additional perspective on Amazon Bedrock as a direction worth considering in the future when expanding Fitness Assistant’s AI capabilities. However, the project hasn’t migrated to Bedrock yet.
6. Agentic Decision Intelligence on AWS This session introduced Agentic Decision Intelligence and how AI Agents support business decision-making. Content included intelligent decision workflows, banking use cases, and Amazon QuickSight.
Key points:
AI Agent is more than a chatbot answering questions. Agent can collect context, analyze data, and support decisions. Workflow based on rules and actual data. Transform data into business insights. Connection to Fitness Assistant:
This session expands how I think about AI in Fitness Assistant. AI Agent could:
Collect context about users (workout history, nutrition, health metrics) Analyze patterns and trends Provide personalized recommendations based on actual data Adjust workout plans based on progress This is an interesting development direction for AI Fitness Assistant in the future - not just answering questions but also proactively analyzing and providing recommendations based on each user’s profile.
7. AWS Principles Beyond AWS: How AWS Knowledge Transfers to Cloud-Native Roles The final session talked about how AWS knowledge isn’t limited to using AWS services. Content included operational principles, release management, incident recovery, security operations, and cloud-native skills.
Key points:
AWS knowledge is the foundation for cloud-native thinking. Principles like automation, infrastructure as code, monitoring, security apply to many platforms. Skills transferable across cloud providers. Connection to internship process:
Through learning AWS during my internship, I realize what’s important isn’t just remembering service names but understanding:
How distributed systems work Security best practices Scalability and high availability Monitoring and observability Deployment strategies Cost optimization Troubleshooting methodology These principles have long-term value, not limited to AWS.

Photo 2: At AWS Office Check-in at FCAJ Community Day August - Bitexco Financial Tower
Photo 3: Pipeline and Release Management Session Session on incident troubleshooting and investigation workflows
Photo 4: Serverless Application Structure Demo Demo of serverless application structure with Lambda function apps
Photo 5: Development Application with AWS Serverless Session introducing Serverless Computing and application patterns
Lessons Learned After attending FCAJ Community Day August, I learned important lessons:
1. AWS architecture is more than deploying applications
A production system needs to simultaneously consider compute, database, monitoring, security, cost, and scalability. We can’t just focus on “code works” while ignoring operational aspects.
2. Serverless is an architecture worth considering for certain workloads
Not every workload needs a continuously running server/service. Serverless can be useful for event-driven tasks, scheduled tasks, background processing, and intermittent workloads. However, trade-offs regarding cold start, execution limits, and stateless design need to be considered before applying to Fitness Assistant.
3. Database needs to be designed for long-term growth
For Fitness Assistant, workout, nutrition, and InBody measurement data can increase very rapidly over time and number of users. Therefore, we need to think early about data lifecycle, retention policy, archiving strategy, performance optimization, and cost management.
4. GenAI production needs more than a model
From the GenAI migration session, an important lesson is that AI production must have guardrails, evaluation framework, monitoring, security, and governance. We can’t just integrate a model API and consider it done. We need to design a complete architecture to ensure the AI system operates stably, safely, and with quality.
5. Observability and troubleshooting are mandatory
The Agentic AIOps session showed the value of logs, metrics, evidence-based analysis, and root cause investigation. This directly relates to what I’m learning about CloudWatch for Fitness Assistant. A good system needs the ability to self-observe and effectively support developers in troubleshooting when issues arise.
6. AI Agents can develop beyond chatbots
Agents can collect context, analyze data, and support decision-making instead of just answering questions. This is an interesting research direction for Fitness Assistant in the future - AI can proactively analyze workout patterns, nutrition trends, and health metrics to provide personalized recommendations.
7. Cloud-native thinking has long-term value
AWS knowledge isn’t just learning how to use AWS Console. Operational principles like automation, infrastructure as code, security, monitoring, cost optimization, and troubleshooting methodology are transferable skills with long-term value in a cloud-native career path.
Personal Contribution I attended FCAJ Community Day August in person as an attendee. Throughout the event, I:
Followed all technical sessions from 09:00 to 12:00 Noted knowledge related to AWS, Serverless, database optimization, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and AIOps Compared acquired knowledge with the Fitness Assistant architecture being implemented during my internship Identified directions needing further research such as Amazon Bedrock, Serverless patterns, data archiving strategies, CloudWatch monitoring, and operational best practices Sessions particularly relevant to the project include:

title: Blog 1: From Local Docker to Amazon ECR
content:
FROM LOCAL DOCKER TO AMAZON ECR – PREPARATION BEFORE DEPLOYING SYSTEM TO ECS Published: August 22, 2026
Blog URL: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1F8v6Qye3F/
Hashtags: #FCAJ #AWS #Docker #AmazonECR #AmazonECS #CloudComputing #FitnessAssistant
Introduction While researching deployment approaches for the Fitness Assistant project to the cloud, I came across an AWS article titled “Automated software delivery using Docker Compose and Amazon ECS”.
Initially, I was looking for this article to understand how a system running with Docker locally would be deployed on AWS, especially when using Amazon ECS.
At first, I thought the flow would be quite simple: if you have Docker, just move the containers to ECS and run them. But after reading more carefully, I realized that before moving to ECS, there’s a quite important step that I hadn’t really paid much attention to before: Docker image management.
Real-world Problem Fitness Assistant currently isn’t just a single application. The project is split into multiple components:
frontend gateway auth-service user-service fitness-service ai-service payment-service gym-service In the local environment, I can run and test these services relatively easily. But when thinking about moving the system to AWS, I started facing a question:
If the services are on my laptop, where will ECS get the application to run?
A simple approach is to create EC2, SSH into the machine, clone the source code, install Docker, then build and run all containers directly on it. This approach is completely feasible.
But I realized that if done this way, the production server would have to handle quite many tasks. The server both contains source code, has to build the application, stores Docker images, and runs containers.
Experiment Objectives At this stage, my goal isn’t to deploy the entire Fitness Assistant to Amazon ECS yet. I want to solve a smaller step first:
How can each service of the project be packaged into a complete Docker image and stored on AWS?
The flow I’m experimenting with is:
Source code → Dockerfile → docker build → Local Docker Image → docker tag → docker push → Amazon ECR Through this part, I want to check several issues:
Can each service’s Dockerfile build successfully? Does the image actually exist locally after building? What is the size of each image? How should images be versioned? How to move images from local machine to Amazon ECR? After pushing, how to verify the image on ECR is the one just built? Architecture Overview After breaking down the problem, I started seeing more clearly the role of each component:
Developer ↓ Source Code ↓ Dockerfile ↓ Docker Build ↓ Docker Image ↓ Amazon ECR ↓ Amazon ECS ↓ Running Container Amazon ECR is not where applications run. ECR is like a repository storing versions of container images.
For example, Fitness Assistant might have:
fitness-assistant/frontend:v1.0.0 fitness-assistant/auth-service:v1.0.0 fitness-assistant/user-service:v1.0.0 This way, building applications and running applications are separated into two clear parts.
Docker and Amazon ECR Experiment Flow First, I prepared production Dockerfiles for each service. Then ran:
docker build to create images on the local machine. After building, I used:
docker images to check if images were actually created and what the size of each image is.
This is when I realized something quite simple but I hadn’t paid much attention to before: “Build successful” message doesn’t mean the image is ready for production.
For example, with the frontend, some Vite environment variables are included during the build process. If the API URL during build is still localhost, Docker can still build the image successfully. But that image clearly isn’t suitable to run in AWS environment yet.
After checking local images, I created corresponding Private Repositories on Amazon ECR. Next:
docker login to give Docker access to ECR. Then I used:
docker tag to attach ECR Repository URI to the image. Finally:
docker push to upload the image to ECR.
After pushing, I didn’t just stop at seeing the terminal report success but continued to check directly on AWS Console. There I could see:
Image tag Image digest Image size Time image was pushed Why Not Deploy Source Code Directly to EC2? This was also a question I asked during the research process. If EC2 is also a server, why not simply create an EC2 instance, install Docker, and run Fitness Assistant directly on it?
From my understanding, this approach isn’t wrong. For a small project, one server, and not many users yet, it’s completely possible:
Source code → EC2 → Docker → Application But with Fitness Assistant currently having many services, I want to separate responsibilities more clearly. If building directly on EC2, then EC2 is both where source code is received, images are built, and containers are run.
With the approach I’m researching:
Source code → Docker image → Amazon ECR → Amazon ECS each part has its own responsibility:
Docker packages the application ECR stores images ECS manages containers What I Found Most Interesting What I found most interesting isn’t the docker push command. But rather how I started viewing Docker images differently.
Previously, I mainly used Docker to:
build images run containers test applications locally But when introducing ECR into the flow, Docker images started looking more like packaged versions of the application.
For example:
auth-service:v1.0.0 auth-service:v1.0.1 These two versions can coexist on ECR. This helps me clearly know what versions the system has instead of overwriting the old image with each update.
Some Notes I Learned from Testing Don’t consider a Docker image complete just because docker build doesn’t error. Need to recheck the configuration inside the image.
Don’t include sensitive files in images. Files like .env, credentials, API Keys shouldn’t appear inside Docker images. Therefore .dockerignore needs to be checked.
Image versioning. If all images use latest, after a while it will be quite difficult to know which image corresponds to which version of source code.
Must verify images after pushing. Shouldn’t just see docker push succeed and conclude the entire test has PASSED.
Personal Perspective Before reading the AWS article, I thought quite simply that if the application was containerized, the next step was just finding a place on AWS to run containers.
But after analyzing the article’s flow, I realized between source code and a container running on cloud, there’s a quite important step which is container image management.
This is also why I didn’t want to go straight to ECS. If deploying frontend, gateway and many backend services to ECS immediately while Dockerfiles still have issues, then I would have to debug Docker, ECR, ECS, networking, load balancer and many other components at the same time.
Instead, I chose to do it step by step:
First ensure: Source code → Docker image works correctly Then: Docker image → Amazon ECR works correctly When these two parts are stable, continue to: Amazon ECR → Amazon ECS Conclusion After this experiment, what I understand more clearly isn’t just how to use Amazon ECR. More importantly, I started seeing clearly the role of Docker images in the process of moving applications from local to cloud.
Docker helps me package applications Amazon ECR helps me store and manage those images Amazon ECS will be the next step to use these images and operate containers on AWS What I learned most from this process is don’t try to deploy the entire architecture from the start. Breaking down each problem, testing each step and understanding clearly the role of each service helps me identify errors more easily and also understand AWS architecture better.
Currently, I’m continuing to refine Docker images of services in Fitness Assistant and test them on Amazon ECR. After this part is stable, my next step will be researching how images in ECR are used to deploy services to Amazon ECS.
Reference Links AWS Containers Blog – Automated software delivery using Docker Compose and Amazon ECS: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/automated-software-delivery-using-docker-compose-and-amazon-ecs Amazon ECR Documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ecr/ Amazon ECS Documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ecs/ Shared on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1F8v6Qye3F/

title: Week 1 Worklog
content:
Week 1 Objectives: Register AWS account for practice, research Free Tier and cost management. Learn and practice the first 5 labs: IAM, VPC, EC2, RDS to master foundational services. Prepare environment to start analyzing Fitness Assistant source code next week. Tasks for This Week: Task Start Date Completion Date Workshop / Reference Materials - Register AWS Free Tier account - Configure IAM user, enable MFA - Learn and practice first 5 labs 08-03-2026 08-08-2026 1: https://000001.awsstudygroup.com/ 2: https://000002.awsstudygroup.com/ 3: https://000003.awsstudygroup.com/ 4: https://000004.awsstudygroup.com/ 5: https://000005.awsstudygroup.com/ - Office registration 08-04-2026 08-04-2026 - - Practice additional lab 10 08-04-2026 08-04-2026 - Week 1 Results: Overview:
This week I successfully set up the AWS environment to start learning. The main focus was getting familiar with the most basic services like IAM, EC2, and RDS through 5 labs on AWS Study Group. Initially overwhelming due to many new concepts, but following step by step made things clearer.
Knowledge Learned:
AWS Account & Free Tier: How to register an account, understand what’s free in Free Tier (EC2 750h/month, RDS 750h/month, S3 5GB). Important to set up Budget alerts from the start to avoid unexpected charges.
IAM (Identity and Access Management): Learned how to create Users, Groups, Policies. Understood why Root account shouldn’t be used for daily work. Enabled MFA for both Root and IAM user for security.
Amazon VPC: Learned about virtual networks on AWS, how to create VPC, Subnet, Security Group. This part was a bit difficult requiring understanding of CIDR, routing tables, but necessary for safe app deployment later.
Amazon EC2: Created first instance (t2.micro in Free Tier), SSH into server, installed nginx as test. EC2 feels like renting a VPS but much more flexible.
Amazon RDS: Initialized PostgreSQL database on RDS, connected from EC2. Understood that RDS automatically backs up, Multi-AZ for high availability but more expensive than self-managed DB.
Hands-on Practice:
Successfully created AWS account, verified with visa card Completed all 5 labs on AWS Study Group from 000001 to 000005 Installed AWS CLI on local machine (Windows), tested basic commands like aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances Created EC2 instance + RDS PostgreSQL, connected 2 services via Security Group Attempted additional lab 10 but blocked due to Free Tier account and outdated lab (service no longer supported) Difficulties Encountered:
Account verification pending: After registration, account was pending verification for nearly 1 day. CloudShell couldn’t be used due to “Your account verification is in progress” error. Had to use AWS CLI as workaround.
IAM Policy JSON syntax: First time writing custom policy in JSON was confusing with many fields: Effect, Action, Resource, Condition. Easy to confuse * wildcard with specific ARN.
Security Group configuration: Inbound/Outbound rules concept was confusing. Especially understanding when to use 0.0.0.0/0 (anywhere) and when to restrict by specific IP.
RDS connection string: Initially couldn’t connect from EC2 to RDS because forgot to config Security Group to allow EC2 security group ID. Had to research security group chaining.
Lab 10 blocked: When trying additional lab 10, encountered errors because lab was outdated (using old service that was updated) and Free Tier account had limited access to some new services. Need to wait for account upgrade or redo lab with new service.
Solutions:
Account verify: Waited 24h for automatic verification, no need to create support case. While waiting, used AWS CLI instead of CloudShell.
IAM Policy: Used AWS Policy Generator UI instead of writing JSON manually. Referenced AWS Managed Policies (AdministratorAccess, PowerUserAccess) to learn structure.
Security Group: Drew diagram to understand traffic flow: Internet → ALB → EC2 → RDS. Each step needs separate security group rule. Practice principle of least privilege.
RDS connection: Instead of using 0.0.0.0/0 for RDS, configured security group rule to allow source as EC2’s security group ID. More secure and follows best practice.
Lab 10: Found new documentation from AWS Documentation or practiced similar services via Console to understand operational principles instead of following old lab.

title: 5.1 Overview
content:
The Problem Fitness Assistant is a real, actively developed open-source application, but it is built and tested only for local development via Docker Compose. There is no existing AWS deployment, CI/CD pipeline, or cloud infrastructure of any kind in the source repository. This workshop closes that gap by deploying a production-shaped, serverless-first version of the application on AWS.
An earlier version of this report planned a simpler EC2 + Docker Compose MVP. That plan was superseded by the serverless architecture described from here on — Lambda-based microservices behind API Gateway, Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless, Amazon Bedrock and OpenSearch Serverless for AI, and ECS Fargate for the one component (Chat) that genuinely needs a long-lived connection. The Proposal and every Workshop page describe what was actually deployed.
Target Users Gym members / fitness app end users tracking workouts, goals, and receiving AI coaching suggestions. Gym owners, personal trainers and administrators managing gyms, contracts and payments. The FCAJ mentor/reviewer evaluating this internship’s execution. Application Features (as actually deployed) User registration and login, JWT-based (auth-service, Lambda). Profile, onboarding, InBody records, PT applications and contracts, with files stored in a private S3 bucket through presigned URLs (user-service, Lambda + jobs Lambda). Exercise catalog, workout plans, workout logging, nutrition and reminders (fitness-service, Lambda + jobs Lambda). AI coaching and plan generation on Amazon Bedrock — Nova Pro for chat/vision, Cohere multilingual embeddings with an OpenSearch Serverless vector store for retrieval (ai-service: HTTP Lambda, SQS-driven Worker, scheduled Jobs). Gym/PT listings and signed QR check-in (gym-service, Lambda + jobs Lambda), and wallet/PT-contract payments through VNPAY, with MoMo/PayOS/ZaloPay supported by the code (payment-service, Lambda + reconciliation job). Real-time chat (chat-service) on Amazon ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer — Socket.IO needs a long-lived connection that a request/response Lambda cannot hold open. The AI coaching feature originally ran on a self-hosted LLM (Ollama) with a Qdrant vector store, as described in Week 8 of the Worklog. On AWS it moved to Amazon Bedrock (apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0, cohere.embed-multilingual-v3) and OpenSearch Serverless, which removes the work of sizing and patching an instance for the model. The InBody photo extraction feature of user-service called the Anthropic API directly in local development; its API key was deliberately not configured on AWS, so that one feature is not enabled in this DEV environment yet. None of the AI features is a substitute for medical advice.
Desired Outcome A working DEV environment reachable over the internet: a static frontend on Amazon S3, an Amazon API Gateway front door, six Lambda-based microservices and one ECS Fargate service behind it, a single Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless cluster holding one logical database per service, and managed AI on Bedrock and OpenSearch Serverless — documented step by step with evidence (console screenshots, policies, environment variables, verification results), not assumptions.
Scope Shared infrastructure: one VPC, private application subnets for Lambda and Fargate, private DB subnets (no internet route), public subnets for the NAT Gateway and the Chat ALB, and a NAT + Internet Gateway pair for outbound calls. Eight deployment blocks documented end to end: Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI (HTTP + Worker + Jobs + vector search), Chat, and the one-off data migration that restored 7 local PostgreSQL databases into Aurora. Frontend: a static build hosted on Amazon S3 (website endpoint over HTTP for now; CloudFront + Origin Access Control is a known follow-up, not yet usable in this account). Components Still Incomplete CI/CD pipeline: not yet built — deployments so far are manual console/CLI steps, captured as they happened. End-to-end validation: Auth and User are fully verified; Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI/Worker/Jobs, Chat and the frontend integration still need a full E2E pass — see 5.5.5. Security follow-ups deliberately postponed: rotating the ADMIN credential and remediating the remaining seed accounts — not blockers for DEV, but tracked. Cost controls: a DEV “sleep” strategy (Aurora to 0 ACU, Chat to 0 tasks, NAT Gateway only when needed) is planned but not yet automated — see 5.7. Deliverables 5.2 Architecture Description — request flows, AWS service choices, security/IAM, scalability and cost. 5.3 Prerequisite — account, region and local tools. 5.4 Deployment Guide — every service, step by step, with the original console screenshots and the exact IAM policies. 5.5 Test & validation — the checks, their expected results and their current status. 5.6 Demo and 5.7 Clean-up. Definition of Done Every AWS service marked “Deployed” in this report is backed by a screenshot, log excerpt or command output in this Workshop. No step claims success without evidence; checks not run yet are labelled as pending rather than passed.

title: 5.2.1 Architecture Overview
content:
Deployment Status Summary Snapshot of the current AWS deployment, migration, and end-to-end (E2E) test status, as recorded in the internal deployment runbook. Statuses reflect only what is evidenced there.
Component AWS Deployment Migration E2E Status Shared Infrastructure (VPC/Subnets/SGs/NAT/IGW) Complete N/A N/A COMPLETE Aurora PostgreSQL Complete Complete — 7/7 service DBs restored Verified COMPLETE Auth Service Deployed Complete Passed (incl. transaction-atomicity fix) COMPLETE User Service Deployed Complete Passed COMPLETE Fitness Service Deployed Complete Pending full E2E NEEDS VERIFICATION Gym Service Deployed Complete Pending full E2E NEEDS VERIFICATION Payment Service Deployed Complete Pending full E2E NEEDS VERIFICATION AI / Worker / Jobs Deployed Complete Pending E2E NEEDS VERIFICATION Chat Service (REST + Socket.IO) Deployed Complete Pending full E2E NEEDS VERIFICATION Frontend (S3) Deployed N/A Pending full integration E2E NEEDS VERIFICATION CI/CD Incomplete N/A N/A INCOMPLETE Database migration verification: 23/23 audited foreign keys applied and validated. ADMIN credential rotation and remaining seed-account remediation were intentionally postponed (not current blockers, but tracked as open security follow-ups).
Components Shared infrastructure
One VPC (fitness-assistant-dev-vpc, 10.0.0.0/16, ap-southeast-1). Two private application subnets (Lambda functions and the Chat Fargate task), two public subnets (only the NAT Gateway and the Chat ALB sit there), and private DB subnets with no internet route at all. One shared Lambda security group, used by every Lambda-based service, plus dedicated security groups for Aurora, the VPC endpoints, the Chat task and the Chat ALB. One Internet Gateway and one NAT Gateway, so Lambdas in the private subnets can reach Amazon Bedrock and other AWS APIs outbound; interface VPC endpoints keep Secrets Manager and OpenSearch Serverless traffic private. Six Lambda-based microservices: Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment and AI, all behind one Amazon API Gateway HTTP API and sharing the VPC and security group above. Together they run 12 long-lived functions — each service has an HTTP function, User/Fitness/Gym/Payment/AI also have a scheduled jobs function, and AI adds a Worker fed by Amazon SQS — plus one migration function per service. Scheduled work is triggered by 13 Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedules.
One ECS Fargate service: Chat, which handles both a REST API and a Socket.IO real-time connection. Socket.IO needs a connection that stays open for the life of a chat session — a shape Lambda’s request/response model does not fit — so Chat runs as a container on Fargate in the private subnets, behind its own internet-facing Application Load Balancer. REST calls reach it through API Gateway (/chat/{proxy+}), Socket.IO connects to the ALB directly.
One Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless cluster (fitness-assistant-dev-aurora), holding one logical database per service rather than one database per cluster:
fitness-assistant-dev-aurora ├── fitness_assistant → Auth ├── fitness_assistant_user → User ├── fitness_assistant_fitness → Fitness ├── fitness_assistant_gym → Gym ├── fitness_assistant_payment → Payment ├── fitness_assistant_ai → AI └── fitness_assistant_chat → Chat Each service’s Lambda (or the Chat Fargate task) reads its own database only, resolved from its own DATABASE_SECRET_ID in Secrets Manager — no service is configured to reach another service’s database directly.
Managed AI: Amazon Bedrock (Nova Pro for chat and vision, Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 for 1024-dimension embeddings) and an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector collection (fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors, NextGen, scaling between 0 and 2 OCU), reached privately through a VPC endpoint.
One static frontend on Amazon S3 (website hosting, HTTP for now — see 5.2.7 for why CloudFront is not yet in front of it).
How This Differs From the Original MVP Plan The earlier version of this Workshop planned a single EC2 host running the whole Docker Compose stack, one Amazon RDS instance, and a self-hosted Ollama + Qdrant pair for AI (Week 6 of the Worklog compares that plan with the chosen design). That plan’s own “Future Architecture” note already named the direction this ended up taking: ECS/Fargate instead of a single host, and Amazon Bedrock instead of self-hosted Ollama. The real architecture went further: Lambda for six of the seven services, Aurora Serverless instead of a single RDS instance, and OpenSearch Serverless instead of Qdrant.
How each service was actually built is documented step by step in the Deployment Guide; the pages from 5.2.2 onward describe the system as it stands now.

title: 5.3.1 AWS account and permissions
content:
AWS account All resources live in a single AWS account used only for this project’s DEV environment. Every resource is named with the fitness-assistant-dev- prefix (and tagged project=fitness-assistant, environment=dev where the console offers tags), which makes the clean-up in 5.7 a matter of filtering by name.
Console identity The deployment was performed from the AWS Management Console with an IAM user (not the root user). That identity needs permission to create and configure the services used in this workshop:
Area Services Compute AWS Lambda, Amazon ECS (Fargate), Amazon ECR API and networking Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API), Elastic Load Balancing (ALB), Amazon VPC (subnets, route tables, NAT/Internet Gateway, security groups, VPC endpoints) Data Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon S3, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless Messaging and scheduling Amazon SQS, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler AI Amazon Bedrock Security and observability AWS IAM (roles and inline policies), Amazon CloudWatch Logs The application itself never runs with these console permissions. Every Lambda function and ECS task gets its own execution role with an inline policy scoped to the exact secrets, queues and functions it uses — see 5.2.5 Security and IAM.
Amazon Bedrock model access (one-time) The AI service uses two Bedrock models:
Purpose Model Model ID used by the code Chat and vision Amazon Nova Pro (APAC cross-region inference profile) apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 Embeddings (1024 dimensions) Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 cohere.embed-multilingual-v3 Cohere is a third-party model offered through AWS Marketplace, so its subscription/EULA has to be accepted once from the console by an administrator. The Lambda runtime roles are deliberately not given aws-marketplace:* permissions to do this themselves. No API key is needed for either model — the Lambdas call Bedrock with their IAM role.
Payment provider credentials The Payment service is configured with PAYMENT_PROVIDER=VNPAY. Provider credentials (VNPAY terminal code and hash secret, and MoMo / PayOS / ZaloPay keys when they are added) are entered only once a real sandbox credential exists, and they are never copied into chat, documentation or source control.

Knowledge Learned:
IAM Roles for Applications: Last week learned IAM users, this week learned IAM Role - how to let EC2 or Lambda access other services (S3, RDS…) without hardcoding access keys. Important best practice for security.
Amazon S3: Understood S3 is object storage, different from block storage (EBS). Did labs creating buckets, uploading files, configuring public access, versioning. S3 is cheap and convenient but need to be careful with permissions.
Cost Optimization & Lightsail: Learned ways to save money when using AWS (Reserved Instance, Spot Instance, S3 Intelligent-Tiering). Lightsail is like a simpler VPS than EC2, fixed monthly price, suitable for small apps.
Auto Scaling: Mechanism to automatically increase/decrease EC2 instances based on load. Combined with Load Balancer to ensure app is always available when traffic spikes. Concepts of Launch Template and scaling policy.
Amazon CloudWatch: Service to monitor metrics (CPU, memory, network) and create alarms. Important to know when app has errors or is overloaded. Can send notifications via SNS.
Route 53: AWS DNS service, learned how to create hosted zone, A records, CNAME. Has Hybrid DNS feature with Route 53 Resolver to connect on-premise DNS with AWS.
AWS CLI: Practiced many CLI commands to manage resources instead of using Console. Faster and can script automation. Learned how to config credentials, use –query to filter JSON output.
Hands-on Practice:
Analyzed workshop template repo, understood folder structure: content/, static/, config.toml. Learned how to use Hugo to generate static site. Completed 7 labs from 000048 to 000011, practiced with IAM Role, S3, Lightsail, Auto Scaling, CloudWatch, Route 53 and AWS CLI. Read personal project source code (fitness-assistant or similar project), noted tech stack: what frontend uses (React/Vue?), backend (Node/Python?), database (PostgreSQL/MySQL?). Listed services/ports: which port frontend runs on, which port backend API, is it microservices or monolith. Visited office for work on Tuesday August 12, familiarized with environment and setup workspace. Read and researched blog “From Development Container to Production-ready Microservices with Docker and Amazon ECR” to prepare for containerizing project later. This blog is good because it clearly explains the flow from local dev with Docker to pushing images to ECR and deploying to production. Started writing first blog post to share AWS learning experience. Difficulties Encountered:
Route 53 domain cost: Want to practice Route 53 fully need to buy domain but domains on Route 53 are a bit expensive ($.12+ for .com). Tried using Freenom free domain but doesn’t integrate well with Route 53.
Auto Scaling policy confusion: There are many types of scaling policies: target tracking, step scaling, simple scaling. Not clear when to use which, how to configure threshold appropriately.
CloudWatch custom metrics: CloudWatch by default only has basic metrics (CPU, network). To monitor app-level metrics (request count, error rate) must push custom metrics yourself, a bit complex.
Source code without .env.example: When reading project source code there was no .env.example file, had to read code to guess what environment variables are needed. Time consuming and error prone.
Distinguishing API routing vs API Gateway: In code there’s Express router (internal routing) but AWS has a service called API Gateway. Initially confused between these 2 concepts when drawing architecture.
Solutions:
Route 53 domain: Temporarily practice with subdomain on free domain or use existing domain. DNS part is mainly understanding concepts of hosted zone, record types, TTL.
Auto Scaling policy: Read AWS docs and best practices. For typical web apps, using target tracking policy with 70% CPU is simplest and most effective. Step scaling is for more complex patterns.
CloudWatch custom metrics: Learned how to use CloudWatch agent or SDK to push metrics from app. But for MVP stage, using basic metrics combined with application logs is sufficient.
Environment variables: Listed all env variables by grepping in code: grep -r "process.env" . or grep -r "os.getenv" .. Created separate note file to track.
API Gateway: Noted clearly: Express router = code logic to route requests in app. API Gateway = AWS managed service for API endpoint, authentication, rate limiting. Two completely different things.

title: 5.4.2 Auth Service and API Gateway
content:
Auth is the first service every user flow depends on, so it was deployed first, together with the HTTP API that all other Lambda services later attach to. Its logical database is fitness_assistant and its secret is fitness-assistant/dev/database.
Step 1 — Run the Auth schema migration A temporary migration Lambda was created following the common pattern (1024 MB, 5 minute timeout, VPC attached, DATABASE_SECRET_ID = fitness-assistant/dev/database) and invoked once. All 7 Prisma migrations were applied.
Once Auth’s own Lambda was verified against Aurora (Step 3), the temporary migration Lambda was deleted.
Step 2 — Force the Auth Lambda to pick up a rotated credential The Auth Lambda caches its database secret per execution environment. After the Aurora password was changed in Secrets Manager, warm containers could still hold the old credential. To force fresh execution environments, add a harmless variable in Lambda → fitness-assistant-dev-auth → Configuration → Environment variables → Edit:
DEPLOY_REVISION = 20260827-1 The code never reads it; changing the configuration is enough to recycle the environments.
Step 3 — Smoke-test a route that really queries the database In fitness-assistant-dev-auth → Test → Create new event (auth-login-db-smoke), send an API Gateway v2.0 event for POST /auth/login with an e-mail address that does not exist:
{ "version": "2.0", "routeKey": "POST /auth/login", "rawPath": "/auth/login", "rawQueryString": "", "headers": { "content-type": "application/json", "accept": "application/json", "host": "example.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com" }, "requestContext": { "accountId": "123456789012", "apiId": "test", "domainName": "example.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com", "domainPrefix": "example", "http": { "method": "POST", "path": "/auth/login", "protocol": "HTTP/1.1", "sourceIp": "127.0.0.1", "userAgent": "AWS-Lambda-Test" }, "requestId": "auth-db-smoke", "routeKey": "POST /auth/login", "stage": "$default", "time": "27/Aug/2026:09:30:00 +0700", "timeEpoch": 1787797800000 }, "body": "{\"email\":\"aws-smoke-nonexistent@example.com\",\"password\":\"NotARealPassword123!\"}", "isBase64Encoded": false } Expected result: statusCode: 401 (invalid credentials). That is a pass: it proves the chain Auth Lambda → Secrets Manager → Prisma Linux engine → Aurora → users table works. The response must not contain P1000, P1001, PrismaClientInitializationError, Can't reach database or relation "users" does not exist. A 400 means the payload shape is wrong; a 500 means reading the CloudWatch log before changing anything.
Keep Aurora’s minimum capacity at 0.5 ACU while services are still being deployed. With 0 ACU the cluster auto-pauses after a few idle minutes, and the resume delay makes the next smoke test look like a failure.
Step 4 — Create the HTTP API with the Auth integration API Gateway → Create API → HTTP API:
API name: fitness-assistant-dev-api, IP address type IPv4. Add integration → type Lambda, region ap-southeast-1, function fitness-assistant-dev-auth, payload format version 2.0. (Never the migration Lambda.) Step 5 — Create explicit public routes On Configure routes, add one route per public endpoint, all pointing at fitness-assistant-dev-auth:
POST /auth/register POST /auth/register/verify POST /auth/login POST /auth/refresh POST /auth/logout POST /auth/verify PATCH /auth/me GET /auth/users PATCH /auth/users/{userId}/role PATCH /auth/users/{userId}/disable PATCH /auth/users/{userId}/enable GET /health These routes are not created: /auth/internal/* (service-to-service endpoints protected by INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, called by other Lambdas through direct invoke instead) and GET /metrics (in-memory Prometheus counters are meaningless when every Lambda execution environment keeps its own). A catch-all ANY /auth/{proxy+} would have been faster, but it would also have published /auth/internal/* to the internet — explicit routes keep the security boundary.
Step 6 — Keep the $default stage with auto-deploy Keep the default $default stage with Auto-deploy enabled, so route changes go live without a manual deployment and the invoke URL stays short.
The API’s invoke URL (https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com) is what the frontend and the PAYMENT_PUBLIC_URL / AUTH_SERVICE_URL variables use from here on.
Step 7 — Allow the S3 frontend to call the API (CORS) After the frontend is published (5.4.3), configure API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → CORS → Configure:
Setting Value Access-Control-Allow-Origin http://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>.s3-website-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com (HTTP, because the S3 website endpoint has no HTTPS) Allow headers authorization, content-type Allow methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS Max age 300 Allow credentials Off — the frontend sends Authorization: Bearer <token>, not cross-site cookies Verification: open the frontend /login, open the browser Network tab and log in with a non-existent e-mail. A 401 {"error":"Invalid credentials"} from API Gateway proves the full path S3 website → API Gateway → Auth Lambda → Prisma → Aurora. A CORS error, 404 or 500 means checking the origin value, the route list and the Lambda log respectively.

title: Blog 2: Challenges and Cost Optimization in AWS Deployment
content:
Challenges and Cost Optimization in AWS Deployment: Lessons Learned from Gymini Status: Technical case study written from the experience of deploying Gymini for this internship.
Shared on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/19qBt1z5fU/
This post follows what is already confirmed elsewhere in this report (linked at each point). The parts about AWS credit running out faster than expected and about adopting CloudFormation are presented as an illustrative case study, reasoned from the real cost profile of the deployed architecture — not a confirmed billing history — and CloudFormation is not currently used for this project (every resource so far was created by hand through the AWS Console, see 5.4). The closing “Evidence and limitations” section lists exactly what is confirmed, what is a reasonable inference, and what is only a proposal.
1. Why deploying a multi-component application is not a one-day job Gymini is not a simple CRUD project. It is a pnpm monorepo with seven Node.js/TypeScript services (Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI, Chat) plus a React frontend, which until recently only ran with Docker Compose on one machine — no public endpoint, no backups, no isolation between components (see Proposal §2).
The gap between “it runs on my machine” and “it operates on the cloud” is exactly the work docker compose up never has to do: provisioning a VPC and subnets, writing an IAM role per service, replacing .env files with managed secrets, reconnecting services that no longer share a hostname, adding health checks, centralizing logs, and re-validating each piece after it moves. The number of containers in an application does not predict deployment time, because most of the time goes into wiring managed services together correctly and checking each step, not into building images.
2. Initial expectations versus deployment reality The initial expectation was simple: finish the code, build the Docker images, deploy to AWS, done — possibly in a day. The real deployment of Gymini followed a different loop entirely: provision infrastructure → configure → deploy → validate → troubleshoot → redeploy → confirm, repeated service by service, spread across 26 August to 23 September 2026 (Worklog, Weeks 4–8) — about four weeks, not one day.
Aspect Initial expectation Practical reality Deployment duration About one day Multiple configuration, testing and troubleshooting cycles over roughly four weeks Infrastructure Basic provisioning Several interdependent components (VPC, IAM, Secrets Manager, Aurora, SQS, EventBridge…) Configuration One-time Adjusted repeatedly, with revisions that had to be redone Testing After deployment Continuous, service by service (5.5) Cost Covered by credits, not a concern Some resources bill hourly whether or not they are used “One day” here is the author’s personal expectation going in, not a general benchmark for every project.
3. Technical challenges actually encountered Networking and security. Every added service meant getting the security groups right: lambda-sg and chat-sg are allowed into aurora-sg on port 5432, vpce-sg allows lambda-sg on port 443 to reach Secrets Manager and OpenSearch through VPC endpoints, and the DB subnets have no route to the internet at all (5.2.5). A security group pointed the wrong way means a Lambda function can’t reach the database, with nothing in the logs saying why.
Container deployment. The Chat service produced the most concrete incident: in revision 1 of its task definition, two secrets (CHAT_DATABASE_URL, INTERNAL_API_SECRET) were entered as Value instead of ValueFrom, so the container received the secret’s name instead of its connection string, and Prisma failed with URL must start with postgresql://. The fix was a new revision using ValueFrom with the full ARN and the JSON key suffix (...:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::), followed by Force new deployment (5.4.10).
Database integration. Seven services share one Aurora cluster but each keeps its own logical database and its own secret. Lambda caches the database secret for as long as its execution environment stays warm, so after rotating the Aurora password, the fix was not to wait — it was editing a harmless environment variable (DEPLOY_REVISION) purely to force AWS to create a new execution environment (5.2.6).
Environment configuration. Each service has its own environment variables and secrets, migration Lambdas were created, run once and deleted, and every configuration fix meant a new task definition revision or a function environment-variable update.
Troubleshooting and redeployment. The most repeated pattern was: read the Stopped reason and the service Events instead of recreating the service, update the task definition, then Force new deployment — and confirm Running 1/1, Healthy before calling it done (5.4.10, step 23).
4. Unexpected AWS credit consumption AWS Free Tier, promotional credits and pay-as-you-go are three different things: the Free Tier is a fixed, per-service free allowance; promotional credit is a balance that gets drawn down against the bill and expires; pay-as-you-go is the default pricing for everything beyond those two. Having credit does not mean the infrastructure is free — it only postpones the point at which real money is charged, and once it runs out, billing reverts to list price.
What is easy to overlook while still configuring and debugging: most resources in this architecture bill by usage (Lambda, API Gateway, SQS, Bedrock per token), but a few bill by the hour, regardless of whether a single request arrives. Per the architecture-level estimate in Proposal §8, those fixed items are: the NAT Gateway (~43 USD/month), Aurora at its minimum capacity (~45–60 USD/month), the Chat Fargate task (~22 USD/month), the Application Load Balancer (~20 USD/month), two interface VPC endpoints (~30–40 USD/month) and public IPv4 addresses (~11 USD/month) — roughly 190–230 USD/month running 24/7, or 60–90 USD/month with a “sleep mode” applied (see also 5.2.7). This is a published architectural estimate, not a confirmed billing line item.
From that figure, a technically plausible mechanism follows: if these fixed-cost resources are left running continuously for several weeks while each service is still being deployed, debugged and redeployed — matching the real deployment cadence in section 2 — the “idle” portion of the bill alone can add up faster than intuition suggests, especially with no spending alert configured yet. This is a possible contributing factor, not an incident confirmed against actual billing data for this project.
5. Root cause analysis Problem Possible cause Impact Evidence Proposed improvement Fully manual deployment through the Console No CI/CD built yet Every change takes manual steps and is hard to repeat identically 5.2.6 lists “No CI/CD yet” Infrastructure as Code (CloudFormation or Terraform) plus a CI/CD pipeline Fixed-cost infrastructure running 24/7 No automated schedule to pause it outside test sessions Cost accrues even when nobody is using the system 5.2.7 lists the “DEV sleep strategy” as “Planned, not yet automated” Automatically scale Aurora to 0 ACU, Chat to 0 tasks, and delete the NAT Gateway between test sessions No spending alerts AWS Budgets not configured Unusual spending is noticed late 5.2.7 lists an “AWS Budgets alert” as planned Turn on AWS Budgets with email/SNS notifications No CloudWatch alarms Not configured Errors, throttling and a full DLQ are not actively reported 5.2.6 lists “No CloudWatch alarms yet” Alarms for Lambda errors/throttles, DLQ depth, Aurora capacity, Chat target health Secret entered with the wrong value type in a task definition Manual console entry with no review step before applying Runtime failure in the container, requiring a new revision to fix 5.4.10 — Lesson learned Review infrastructure changes through a Change Set (CloudFormation) or a pull request (Terraform) before applying The table deliberately separates operational causes (not yet automated, no alerting) from the normal cost of running AWS services — not every deployment mistake translates into extra billing, and not every fixed cost is itself a “mistake.”
6. AWS CloudFormation as a proposed solution Infrastructure as Code (IaC) addresses exactly this class of problem: instead of remembering and repeating dozens of console steps, the infrastructure is described in files that can be reviewed before they are applied and reproduced identically in another environment.
AWS CloudFormation manages infrastructure as stacks: a template (YAML or JSON) describes the resources to create, accepts parameters so it can be reused across environments, returns outputs that other stacks can reference, and supports Change Sets — a preview of exactly what will be created, changed or deleted before anything is actually applied (Change Sets documentation). CloudFormation also supports drift detection, to notice when someone has edited a resource directly outside the stack.
Technical clarification: CloudFormation does not automatically reduce cost — it manages infrastructure as code and makes cleanup of stack-managed resources easier and more consistent. Deleting a stack (deletion documentation) also does not guarantee every related resource disappears — retention policies, snapshots, resources created outside the stack, or a failed deletion can all leave something that needs manual cleanup.
An illustrative directory layout for this direction:
infrastructure/ ├── cloudformation/ │ ├── network.yaml │ ├── security.yaml │ ├── database.yaml │ ├── application.yaml │ └── monitoring.yaml ├── environments/ │ ├── dev/ │ ├── staging/ │ └── production/ └── README.md This layout is illustrative only — the repository has no infrastructure/ directory today, because everything so far was created by hand through the console, as described in 5.4. The project’s most recent target-architecture diagram (Proposal §3) actually names Terraform as its IaC choice; CloudFormation is an equivalent option, tied directly to AWS without an external tool.
graph LR GIT["Git repository"] --> TPL["CloudFormation templates"] TPL --> CS["Change setsreview before apply"] CS --> CF["AWS CloudFormation"] CF --> DEV["Stack: Development"] CF --> STG["Stack: Staging"] CF --> PRD["Stack: Production"] Figure 3 — Infrastructure management lifecycle with CloudFormation: changes are reviewed through a Change Set before being applied, and each environment is its own stack.
7. Separating Dev, Staging and Production Today the project has only one DEV environment (5.5.5), so this section is a proposal, not the current state.
Development — minimal infrastructure where technically feasible, cost-conscious configuration, temporary resources with controlled cleanup. Staging — integration testing, deployment validation, production-like configuration where it matters, kept controlled enough to avoid unnecessary spend. Production — reliability, security, scalability, monitoring and data protection come first. Identical configuration across all three environments is unnecessarily expensive, but cutting configuration down to the point where it compromises functionality, security or test fidelity is not optimization either — the trade-off has to be deliberate, not arbitrary.
8. Cost optimization strategy Cost visibility — AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets with alerts, cost allocation tags per service (both currently open items, see section 5). Infrastructure lifecycle — the existing consistent naming convention (fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-...) already makes resources filterable by owner; what is missing is a stack-based deletion workflow and a cleanup-confirmation step, matching the full teardown order already documented in 5.7. Right-sizing — choices already applied: Aurora Serverless v2 with a 0.5 ACU floor, Lambda at 1024 MB, OpenSearch Serverless at 0–2 OCU, Fargate at 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB for Chat (5.2.7). Automation — integrating IaC into CI/CD (not yet built), scheduled shutdown of DEV resources outside test hours where technically supported, and a cleanup procedure for failed deployments. Governance — documented cost ownership, a pre-deployment checklist, environment naming conventions, budget thresholds, and a regular billing review. A budget alert is not instantaneous — it should be treated as an early signal to investigate, not a hard spending cap that can never be exceeded.
9. Current state versus proposed target state Criterion Current state (confirmed) Proposed target Infrastructure provisioning Manual, through the AWS Console (5.4) Infrastructure as Code Environment configuration Documented step by step, not parameterized Parameterized, reusable across environments Resource tracking Manual inspection by naming convention Stack-based visibility plus resource tags Redeployment Force new deployment, repeated troubleshooting (5.4.10) Controlled updates through Change Sets Cost monitoring No Budgets or Alarms yet (5.2.6, 5.2.7) Proactive alerts and periodic review Cleanup A documented checklist exists, not yet run (5.7) Stack-based cleanup with a confirmation step Reproducibility Limited, depends on the operator Infrastructure under version control This compares the confirmed current state against a proposed target, not the measured result of a completed migration.
10. Lessons learned Cloud deployment is an engineering process, not the final step after the code is done. Infrastructure cost should be estimated before provisioning, not discovered after the bill arrives — the budget table in Proposal §8 belongs at the start, not written after the fact. A development environment should be designed around what it actually needs operationally, not copied from production. Automated infrastructure management reduces configuration drift — the Chat service’s Value-versus-ValueFrom secret error is a concrete example of where manual steps go wrong. Resource lifecycle management matters as much as initial provisioning — a resource with no cleanup plan eventually costs more than expected. Free credit should be budgeted like a limited resource, not treated as unlimited. Deployment readiness includes operational and cost visibility, not just an application that starts. Infrastructure as Code contributes to long-term maintainability and reproducibility. 11. Future improvement roadmap Phase 1 — Infrastructure audit (partially in place): inventory resources by the existing naming convention, use the published estimate in Proposal §8, review the security gaps already recorded in 5.2.5 — still missing: a review of actual billing over time.
Phase 2 — CloudFormation adoption (not started): write templates per resource group (network, security, database, application, monitoring), parameterize by environment, test both deployment and stack deletion.
Phase 3 — Cost governance (not started, has a foundation): turn on AWS Budgets, extend the existing naming convention into resource tags, write a lifecycle policy for non-production environments, schedule regular cost reviews.
Phase 4 — Deployment automation (not started): integrate IaC into CI/CD, use Change Sets to review infrastructure before applying it, add post-deployment verification, and build rollback and cleanup procedures for failed deployments.
Diagrams graph LR A["Application code"] --> B["Docker build"] B --> C["Deploy to AWS"] C --> D{"Health check"} D -- fail --> E["Debug"] E --> F["Fix configuration"] F --> G["Redeploy"] G --> D D -- pass --> H["Monitor"] Figure 1 — The deployment debugging loop: every failed health check triggers a round of debugging, fixing configuration and redeploying, and each round costs both engineering time and running-resource time.
graph LR subgraph AlwaysOn ["Infrastructure running 24/7 regardless of traffic — conceptual"] NAT["NAT Gateway"] ALB["Chat ALB"] FG["Fargate task"] AU["Aurora, minimum capacity"] VE["VPC interface endpoints"] IP["Public IPv4 addresses"] end NAT --> SUM["Monthly costsee Proposal §8"] ALB --> SUM FG --> SUM AU --> SUM VE --> SUM IP --> SUM SUM -. if left running for weeks .-> CREDIT["Free or promotional creditcan deplete faster than expected"] Figure 2 — A conceptual diagram, not a real billing chart, showing why hourly-billed resources can add up quickly if left running while the system is still being configured and tested.
Evidence and limitations Confirmed in this report: the seven-service plus AI plus Chat architecture; manual console-based deployment spanning 26 Aug – 23 Sep 2026; the Chat service’s Value-versus-ValueFrom secret error and its fix; Lambda’s secret caching behavior and the DEPLOY_REVISION workaround; the absence of CI/CD and CloudWatch alarms; the published budget estimate of ~190–230 USD/month (24/7) or ~60–90 USD/month (sleep mode); the full clean-up order in 5.7, not yet executed. Reported experience, without logs or billing attached in this report: the general deploy-test-fix-redeploy cadence across weeks. Possible contributing factor, not confirmed by billing data: fixed-cost infrastructure running continuously during debugging depleting credit faster than expected. Proposed, not yet implemented: the entire CloudFormation section, Dev/Staging/Production separation, AWS Budgets, CloudWatch Alarms, a scheduled shutdown for idle infrastructure. Already applied in practice (unrelated to CloudFormation): pay-per-invocation Lambda, Aurora Serverless v2 with a low capacity floor, OpenSearch Serverless at 0–2 OCU, a single shared NAT Gateway, a right-sized Fargate task for Chat — see 5.2.7. title: Proposal
content:
Gymini — AI Fitness Assistant on AWS A serverless microservices deployment with managed AI on Amazon Bedrock 1. Executive Summary Gymini (the open-source Fitness Assistant project) is a pnpm monorepo with a React/Vite frontend and seven Node.js/TypeScript services — Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI and Chat — that until now only ran on a developer machine with Docker Compose. This internship project designs and deploys it on AWS as a serverless-first DEV environment in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) region, documented step by step so it can be reviewed, repeated and later automated.
Each service runs on the AWS service that fits its runtime shape: six request/response services on AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway, the real-time Chat service on Amazon ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, one Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 cluster with a logical database per service, Amazon Bedrock (Nova Pro, Cohere Embed) and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for the AI coach, and Amazon SQS plus EventBridge Scheduler for background work. The static frontend is served from Amazon S3; credentials live in AWS Secrets Manager; every function has its own least-privilege IAM role inside private subnets.
At the latest checkpoint every service is deployed, the 7 local databases have been restored into Aurora with all 23 audited foreign keys validated, and Auth and User pass end-to-end tests. Remaining work — end-to-end tests of the other services, CI/CD, alarms, HTTPS and an automated “sleep” mode for cost — is planned and tracked in the Workshop.
2. Problem Statement Current problems Local-only operation. The whole stack (PostgreSQL, Redis, Qdrant, a self-hosted Ollama model and seven services) runs in Docker Compose on one laptop: no public endpoint, no backups, no isolation between components. Secrets in .env files. Database passwords, JWT and service-to-service secrets and provider keys are plain text on disk. Heavy self-hosted AI. The AI coach needs a local LLM and vector database on an always-on machine; an earlier EC2 sizing exercise showed that a free-tier instance cannot run it. Background work tied to processes. Reminders, settlements and reconciliation ran as in-process timers, which do not exist on serverless compute. Real-time chat. Socket.IO needs long-lived connections that a request/response platform cannot hold. Proposed solution Re-platform each part onto the managed service that matches it, adapting the code where needed:
Request/response services → AWS Lambda with HTTP API (payload 2.0) handlers, a separate jobs handler and a migration handler that reads DATABASE_SECRET_ID; internal calls become direct Lambda invokes instead of HTTP through an application gateway. Real-time chat → ECS Fargate behind an ALB, REST routed through API Gateway. PostgreSQL → Aurora Serverless v2, one logical database per service, data restored from the local dumps. AI → Amazon Bedrock for chat, vision and embeddings; OpenSearch Serverless for vectors; long generations queued on SQS and processed by a worker. Timers → EventBridge Scheduler schedules invoking jobs functions. Frontend → S3 static website (CloudFront and HTTPS as the next step). Benefits The DEV environment pays mostly for what it uses, there are no servers to patch for six of the seven services, the AI coach no longer needs a model host, networking is private and permissions are least-privilege by default, and the deployment is captured in a runbook that can be repeated by hand or turned into a pipeline.
3. Solution Architecture The diagram shows the architecture this project is designed around. It is the target the deployment works toward; Workshop 5.5.5 tracks exactly which pieces are confirmed running in the DEV environment today, and Workshop 5.2 has the full description — request flows, service selection, security, scalability and cost.

API layer — a single Amazon API Gateway REST API, with one route group per service (/auth/*, /users/*, /fitness/*, /payments/*, /gyms/*, /ai/*, /health). Serverless backend — six AWS Lambda services (Auth, User, Fitness, Payment, Gym, AI), deployed across multiple Availability Zones by default. Data — Aurora Serverless v2 (PostgreSQL) with a primary and a replica across two private DB subnets, Multi-AZ replication, and an optional Amazon RDS Proxy in front of it. Shared services — an S3 uploads bucket, Secrets Manager for credentials, and CloudWatch for logs and metrics. Asynchronous and AI processing — Amazon EventBridge for schedules and events, Amazon SQS feeding a Lambda worker, which calls Amazon Bedrock for generation and an OpenSearch Serverless vector store for retrieval. DevOps — GitHub source code, a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline authenticating through OIDC, and Terraform as infrastructure as code. Monitoring — CloudWatch logs, metrics, alarms and dashboards, Amazon SNS for alerts, AWS X-Ray for tracing, and AWS Budgets / Cost Explorer for cost control. Network — everything outside the Edge and DevOps groups runs in a VPC spread across multiple Availability Zones, with no EC2 instances or containers in this design. 4. AWS Services Used Service Role in the system Amazon S3 Static frontend hosting; private uploads (presigned URLs); Lambda deployment artifacts; database migration dumps Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Public REST entry point with explicit routes, CORS, AI route throttling and an HTTP proxy to the Chat ALB AWS Lambda Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment and AI services (HTTP, jobs and worker functions) and per-service schema migrations Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate Chat service (REST + Socket.IO) and the one-shot database migrator task Amazon ECR Private container images for Chat and the migrator Elastic Load Balancing (ALB) Socket.IO/WebSocket entry for Chat, /health checks, stickiness, rules hiding internal paths Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 Relational data for all services, one logical database each Amazon Bedrock Nova Pro for chat and vision; Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 for embeddings Amazon OpenSearch Serverless Vector search for RAG and knowledge retrieval Amazon SQS AI task queue and dead-letter queue Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Schedules for settlements, reminders, payouts, reconciliation and AI jobs AWS Secrets Manager Database credentials, the Chat database URL and the shared internal secret AWS IAM Per-function execution roles, ECS task/execution roles, scheduler roles Amazon VPC Network isolation: subnets, route tables, security groups NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway Outbound internet access for the private subnets VPC interface endpoints Private access to Secrets Manager and OpenSearch Serverless Amazon CloudWatch Logs Logs for every function, the Chat task and the migrator AWS Marketplace One-time subscription to the Cohere model on Bedrock 5. Component Design Frontend (React/Vite) — S3 website; REST calls to API Gateway with a Bearer token; Socket.IO to the Chat ALB; user-facing handling of 429/408/504 from the AI routes. Auth service — registration, verification, login, refresh, logout, user administration; database fitness_assistant. User service — profile, onboarding, InBody records, PT applications, contracts, sessions, availability, notifications; uploads to private S3 prefixes; jobs: session settlement, auto-confirm, reschedule expiry; database fitness_assistant_user. Fitness service — exercises, workouts, nutrition, food, training cycles, coach data, equipment, imports/exports, templates, statistics; jobs: upcoming and unfinished workout reminders; database fitness_assistant_fitness. Gym service — gyms, PT listings, owner and admin tools, collaborations, signed QR check-in; jobs: membership payouts, referral settlement; database fitness_assistant_gym. Payment service — payments, wallet, PT wallet, withdrawals, admin payments, provider callbacks (VNPAY by default; MoMo, PayOS, ZaloPay supported); job: reconciliation every 5 minutes; database fitness_assistant_payment. AI service — HTTP function (/ai, /plans, /marketplace, /admin/ai), SQS worker for long generations, jobs function for auto-accept and nightly knowledge ingestion; Bedrock and OpenSearch; database fitness_assistant_ai. Chat service — conversations and real-time messaging on Fargate; database fitness_assistant_chat. Migration — one migration function per service (Prisma migrate deploy) and a Fargate task that restored the local data. Aurora cluster — fitness-assistant-dev-aurora, seven logical databases. Vector collection — fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors with the exercises, fitness_knowledge, fitness_faq and fitness_evidence indexes (1024 dimensions, FAISS/HNSW, cosine similarity). 6. Technical Implementation Implementation phases Analysis and code adaptation — audit every service; add Lambda HTTP, jobs and migration handlers; read credentials through DATABASE_SECRET_ID; replace internal HTTP calls with direct Lambda invokes; add SQS, Bedrock and OpenSearch providers; build artifacts that bundle the Prisma Linux engine. Shared foundation — VPC, subnets, security groups, NAT and Internet Gateway, Aurora Serverless v2, Secrets Manager endpoint. First service and entry points — Auth Lambda, API Gateway with explicit routes, S3 website, CORS. Core services — User, Fitness, Gym and Payment with their jobs functions and schedules, then the Gym ↔ Payment wiring. AI — Bedrock models, SQS worker, jobs function, OpenSearch Serverless, knowledge schedules, AI routes with throttling, Payment → AI activation. Real time and data — Chat on ECS Fargate behind an ALB; restore of the 7 local databases with a Fargate migrator. Validation and hardening — end-to-end tests, alarms, CI/CD, HTTPS with CloudFront, cost “sleep” automation. The exact console steps for phases 2–6, with screenshots and IAM policies, are in the Deployment Guide.
Technical requirements Compute — Lambda Node.js 22.x on x86_64 with 1024 MB; timeouts of 30 s for HTTP, 1 minute for jobs, 300 s for the AI worker, 600 s for AI jobs and up to 15 minutes for migrations; Fargate task of 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB. API — HTTP API with payload format 2.0; no /internal/*, /metrics or catch-all routes; throttling of 1 request/s (burst 3) on the AI routes. Data — Prisma migrations applied per service; one logical database per service; SQS visibility timeout 600 s with a DLQ after 2 receives. AI — Bedrock in ap-southeast-1 through the APAC inference profile; 1024-dimension embeddings; OpenSearch FAISS/HNSW with cosine similarity. Security — least-privilege IAM per function; credentials in Secrets Manager; private subnets and security-group-to-security-group rules; no secrets in artifacts, images or documentation. Operations — CloudWatch Logs; every manual step documented, to be replaced by a CI/CD pipeline. 7. Timeline & Milestones The internship runs from 3 August to 19 October 2026. Dates below are taken from the resources’ creation dates in the deployment runbook.
Phase Period Main activities 1. Learning and analysis August 2026 (weeks 1–3) AWS fundamentals (FCJ modules), application audit, local run, deployment design 2. Foundation and first service 26–27 August 2026 (week 4) VPC and NAT, Aurora, Auth Lambda, API Gateway, S3 frontend; User database and role 3. Core services 2–8 September 2026 (weeks 5–6) Fitness (2 Sep), Gym and Payment (8 Sep) with their jobs and schedules 4. AI 15 September 2026 (week 7) Bedrock, SQS worker, jobs, OpenSearch Serverless, knowledge schedules, AI routes 5. Chat and data 22–23 September 2026 (week 8) Chat on ECS Fargate behind an ALB; migrator image and restore of the 7 databases 6. Validation and report October 2026 (weeks 10–12) End-to-end tests and fixes, CI/CD, alarms, cost controls, report and clean-up 8. Budget Estimation Monthly estimate for the DEV environment in ap-southeast-1 running 24×7 with light test traffic. Figures are approximate on-demand list prices and change over time — confirm them with the AWS Pricing Calculator; the account’s real bill in Cost Explorer is the reference.
Cost group Estimated configuration Monthly cost (USD) NAT Gateway 1 gateway × 730 h, plus data processed ~43 + data Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 0.5 ACU floor × 730 h (≈365 ACU-hours), small storage ~45–60 ECS Fargate (Chat) 0.5 vCPU + 1 GB × 730 h ~22 Application Load Balancer 1 ALB × 730 h, low LCU usage ~20 Public IPv4 addresses NAT Elastic IP + 2 ALB addresses × 730 h ~11 Interface VPC endpoints Secrets Manager and OpenSearch, 2 AZs each ~30–40 OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) 0–2 OCU, scales to 0 when idle depends on active hours Amazon Bedrock Nova Pro and Cohere Embed, per token, test volume ~1–10 AWS Lambda ~40,000 scheduled invocations + test traffic, 1 GB ~0 (free tier) API Gateway (HTTP API) < 1 million requests ~0–1 Secrets Manager 9 secrets ~4 S3, ECR, CloudWatch Logs, SQS, EventBridge small volumes ~2–5 Estimated total: about USD 190–230 per month if everything runs 24×7. With the planned sleep mode — Aurora at 0 ACU, the Chat service at 0 tasks and the NAT Gateway removed outside test sessions — about USD 60–90 per month. The fixed hourly items (NAT, ALB, Fargate, Aurora floor, endpoints, IPv4) dominate; the usage-based services cost almost nothing at DEV volume.
9. Risk Assessment Risk Impact Probability Mitigation strategy Idle DEV resources keep billing (NAT, Aurora floor, Fargate, ALB, endpoints) Medium High Sleep mode, AWS Budgets alert, dependency-ordered clean-up Runaway Bedrock usage from a client or frontend bug Medium Medium Route throttling on the AI routes, 429 handling in the frontend, SQS dead-letter queue A secret leaks through screenshots, documents or function configuration High Low–Medium Secrets Manager for credentials, pixel-level redaction of evidence, moving internal secrets from Lambda configuration to Secrets Manager Manual deployments drift or cannot be repeated Medium High Step-by-step runbook with screenshots; CI/CD planned Data migration overwrites or corrupts data High Low Read-only preflight, dumps kept in a private versioned bucket, migration history preserved, foreign-key and row-count verification Single Chat task and HTTP-only endpoints Medium Medium Acceptable for DEV; shared Socket.IO adapter before scaling; domain, ACM certificate and CloudFront for HTTPS Costs and errors are reviewed in Cost Explorer and CloudWatch Logs after each test session until alarms are in place.
If something goes wrong, the frontend can be rolled back from its S3 backup, a Lambda can be re-uploaded with its previous artifact, a Fargate service can be pointed back to an earlier task definition revision, and the databases can be rebuilt from the migration dumps.
10. Expected Outcomes Immediate results: a working DEV environment on AWS for the whole application — frontend, six Lambda services, real-time chat, managed AI and the restored data — with a reproducible deployment guide and recorded verification results (Workshop 5.5).
Technical learning: practical experience with serverless design on Lambda, API Gateway and EventBridge; containers on ECS Fargate and ECR; Aurora Serverless and data migration; managed AI with Bedrock and OpenSearch Serverless; and the network and IAM boundaries that keep all of it private and least-privilege.
Longer term: the same design can grow into a production environment by adding a CI/CD pipeline and infrastructure as code, HTTPS with CloudFront and WAF, CloudWatch alarms, auto scaling for Chat with a shared Socket.IO adapter, and separate DEV/production accounts.
