This week learned about migration - ways to move systems to AWS. Although my project is built new from scratch, understanding migration is still useful, especially DMS might be helpful later. Also started learning how to package Docker for production.
Knowledge Learned:
1. AWS Migration - 7Rs
AWS has 7 migration strategies:
Rehost: Move as-is to cloud, fast but not optimized Relocate: Move VMware workload to VMware Cloud on AWS Replatform: Minor changes to use managed services (RDS…) Refactor: Rewrite app cloud-native (containers, serverless) Repurchase: Switch to SaaS instead of self-host Retire: Shut down unused apps Retain: Keep on-premise My project uses Refactor from start since building new.
2. VM Import/Export
Through lab 14 learned VM import flow:
Export VM from VMware/Hyper-V → virtual disk (VMDK, VHD) Upload disk to S3 Use aws ec2 import-image to create AMI Launch EC2 from AMI Key points:
IAM role vmimport must have trust policy and S3 permissions, missing causes InvalidParameter error Disk format must be supported (VMDK, VHD, VHDX, OVA) S3 bucket same region as EC2 3. Database Migration
AWS SCT:
Converts schema between DB engines (Oracle → PostgreSQL…) Assessment report shows what can be auto-converted vs manual Complex stored procedures usually need manual rewrite AWS DMS:
DMS has 3 migration types:
Full load: Migrate all data, use when have downtime Full load + CDC: Migrate data first, then sync changes continuously to reduce downtime CDC only: Only sync changes from a point in time DMS components:
Source/Target endpoints Replication instance (EC2 running DMS) Replication task Monitoring:
Important metrics:
CDCLatencySource/Target: Latency capturing/applying changes CPU/Memory/Disk I/O of replication instance Network throughput If CDC latency high, need to check CPU, memory, I/O, network, source workload before deciding to scale instance.
Multi-AZ: Only for high availability, not performance fix.
4. Docker Production
Multi-stage build:
Pattern separating build and runtime:
# Build stage FROM node:20-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci && npm run build # Runtime stage FROM node:20-alpine COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"] Smaller image without dev deps and source code.
Frontend static + Nginx:
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder RUN npm ci && npm run build FROM nginx:1.25-alpine COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html Runtime only needs Nginx, no Node.
Base image:
Alpine: Small but uses musl libc, sometimes native modules fail Debian slim: Larger but better compatibility Node version:
Node 18 EOL (04/2025), don’t use for production Node 20 LTS until 04/2026 Should consider Node 22 LTS Notes:
Must have .dockerignore Run as non-root user Don’t hardcode secrets in image 5. Completed Blog 1
Finished writing first blog post about AWS learning experience and shared on Facebook group. The post summarizes what was learned from weeks 1-3, labs completed, and some tips for AWS beginners.
Blog link: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1F8v6Qye3F/

title: 5.2.3 Main Request Flows
content:
Core API path Covers Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment and the AI HTTP Lambda.
The browser loads the static frontend from the Amazon S3 website endpoint. The frontend calls Amazon API Gateway (fitness-assistant-dev-api) with Authorization: Bearer <JWT>. API Gateway matches the route (explicit routes for Auth, one root + greedy route pair per prefix for the other services) and invokes the service’s Lambda with payload format 2.0. /internal/*, /metrics and a catch-all /{proxy+} are never published. The Lambda verifies the JWT itself — the AI Lambda, for example, invokes the Auth Lambda to validate the token and rejects spoofed x-user-id / x-user-role headers — so there is no separate API Gateway authorizer. When a request needs another service, the Lambda invokes that service’s Lambda directly (lambda:InvokeFunction), authenticated with the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET. Examples: User → Auth, Payment → Auth/User/Gym, Gym → Payment, Payment → AI to activate a paid personalized service. The Lambda reads/writes its own logical database on Aurora through the private app subnets, using credentials it resolves from Secrets Manager at runtime. The response returns through API Gateway to the browser. Chat path REST (conversation lists, history): the frontend calls API Gateway ANY /chat/{proxy+}, an HTTP proxy integration that forwards to http://<chat-alb>/chat/{proxy}. Real-time: the frontend opens Socket.IO directly to the Chat ALB (/socket.io/), HTTP on port 80 in DEV. The ALB forwards to the Fargate task on container port 3005; its listener answers /internal/* and /metrics with a fixed 404 so they never reach the container. Target-group stickiness keeps a client on the same task. The task runs in the private app subnets with no public IP; its security group only accepts port 3005 from the ALB’s security group. The Chat Service reads/writes fitness_assistant_chat on Aurora and invokes the Auth/User Lambdas through its ECS task role. DEV runs the ALB on HTTP only, like the S3 website endpoint, so there is no mixed-content problem yet. Moving both to HTTPS needs a domain and an ACM certificate (see 5.2.5).
Background path Scheduled jobs — 13 EventBridge Scheduler schedules (session settlement, auto-confirm, reschedule expiry, workout reminders, membership payouts, referral settlement, payment reconciliation, AI auto-accept and four nightly knowledge refreshes) invoke each service’s jobs Lambda with a {"job": "<name>"} payload. Each service has its own scheduler role that can invoke only its own jobs function. Long AI work — the AI HTTP Lambda queues plan generations on Amazon SQS (fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks); the AI Worker Lambda consumes them one at a time (batch size 1, up to 300 s each, 2 attempts before the dead-letter queue) and the frontend polls the job status. Knowledge ingestion — the AI Jobs Lambda fetches PubMed, RSS, web and local evidence nightly, embeds it with Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 (1024 dimensions) and writes it to OpenSearch Serverless. All AI functions call Amazon Bedrock through the NAT Gateway and reach OpenSearch Serverless privately through its VPC endpoint, signing requests with their IAM role (SigV4). Why three separate paths instead of one The Core API path is a textbook fit for Lambda: short-lived, stateless, scales to zero. The Chat path cannot use that model because Socket.IO needs a connection that survives many request/response cycles — hence ECS Fargate and an ALB for that one service. The Background path keeps slow or periodic work out of a user’s HTTP request: API Gateway gives an integration about 30 seconds, while a plan generation can take minutes and a knowledge crawl up to ten.

title: 5.3.3 Local tools
content:
The deployment was run from a Windows workstation with PowerShell. The tools below are needed to build the artifacts that the console steps upload.
Tool Used for Git Cloning the application repository (fitness-assistant) Node.js 22 + pnpm Building each service and producing its Lambda ZIP artifacts under backend/services/<service>/artifacts/ (Lambda runtime is Node.js 22.x) AWS CLI v2 aws ecr get-login-password, aws s3 sync for the frontend, and aws ecs run-task for the data migration Docker Desktop Building the Chat Service image and the database migrator image for linux/amd64 and pushing them to Amazon ECR A browser with developer tools Checking API calls from the S3-hosted frontend (Network tab, CORS errors, HTTP 401/429 responses) Build artifacts per service Each backend service produces separate artifacts for its HTTP handler, its background jobs and its schema migration, all from the same build:
Artifact Handler Purpose <service>-lambda.zip dist/lambda.handler HTTP API (API Gateway payload format 2.0) <service>-lambda.zip (same ZIP) dist/jobs-lambda.handler Scheduled jobs invoked by EventBridge Scheduler <service>-migrate-lambda.zip dist/migrate-lambda.handler Creates the service’s logical database if missing and runs prisma migrate deploy ai-worker-lambda.zip dist/worker-lambda.handler AI Worker consuming the SQS queue ZIPs larger than the direct-upload limit (for example the ~69 MiB migration artifacts) are uploaded to the deployments bucket fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id> first and attached to the function with Upload from → Amazon S3 location. Every artifact bundles the Prisma query engine for Linux (rhel-openssl-3.0.x), so the same ZIP built on Windows runs on Lambda.
Never put .env files, database passwords, JWT_SECRET, INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, AWS credentials or payment provider keys into an artifact, an image or an S3 bucket. All of them are resolved at runtime from AWS Secrets Manager or the function configuration.

title: 5.4.3 Frontend on Amazon S3
content:
The React (Vite) frontend is a static build, so it is served straight from an S3 website endpoint: http://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>.s3-website-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com.
This is a temporary DEV setup because Amazon CloudFront was not usable in this account at the time. The bucket is made publicly readable (objects only) so the website endpoint can serve it. Once CloudFront is available, the bucket goes back to private behind an Origin Access Control and the site moves to HTTPS.
Step 1 — Enable static website hosting S3 → Buckets → fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id> → Properties → Static website hosting → Edit:
Setting Value Static website hosting Enable Hosting type Host a static website Index document index.html Error document index.html Using index.html as the error document matters: the frontend uses React Router (createBrowserRouter), so refreshing /login, /register or /client/dashboard must return the app instead of an S3 404.
Step 2 — Allow public reads for this bucket only Permissions → Block public access (bucket settings) → Edit, untick Block all public access, and confirm the warning.
Then Bucket policy → Edit with a policy that allows nothing but s3:GetObject on this bucket’s objects:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>/*" } ] } The public can GET index.html and assets/*; it cannot PutObject, DeleteObject or ListBucket.
Step 3 — Upload the build Upload the contents of frontend/web/dist/ (index.html and assets/).
Verification: /login loads directly from the website endpoint, which confirms the React build, S3 static hosting and the SPA fallback. API calls from the page only work after the CORS step in 5.4.2.
Redeploy procedure Used every time a backend endpoint the frontend depends on changes — for example after the Chat ALB was created in 5.4.10. Run from frontend/web:
1. Build and check that the bundle points at the right backends.
npm run build Select-String -Path ".\dist\assets\*.js" -Pattern "<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com" Select-String -Path ".\dist\assets\*.js" -Pattern "fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb" Both searches must return at least one match.
2. Back up the current site before overwriting it.
$backup = "..\..\backups\frontend-s3-before-chat-20260922" New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $backup | Out-Null aws s3 sync s3://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id> $backup Get-ChildItem $backup 3. Publish the new build and stop browsers from caching the old index.html.
aws s3 sync .\dist s3://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id> --delete aws s3 cp .\dist\index.html s3://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>/index.html ` --content-type "text/html" ` --cache-control "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate" --delete removes old hashed bundles that are no longer in dist/; the backup makes that safe to roll back. Finish with a hard refresh (Ctrl + Shift + R) on the website endpoint.

title: Blog 3: Secure Multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions
content:
Secure Multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions Original article: Secure multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions (AWS Architecture Blog, 22 June 2026)
In a generative AI assistant shared by a whole company, every department wants answers from the same pool of documents, but not every employee should see every document. Finance reports belong to finance and HR files to HR, while managers may need to read across departments. A recent post on the AWS Architecture Blog shows how to enforce this inside one shared knowledge base, by deciding at retrieval time which documents each user is allowed to use.
1. Why the obvious approaches do not scale One knowledge base per department: the isolation is clear, but cost and operations grow with every new team. Filters hard-coded in the application: a metadata filter such as department = finance works, but every rule change means editing code and redeploying. No central record of decisions: when access logic is spread across code, it is hard to answer “why could this user see that document?”. 2. The solution: one knowledge base, two authorization layers All documents live in one Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and carry a department metadata attribute. Access rules are written as Cedar policies in Amazon Verified Permissions and evaluated on every request:
Layer 1, API access. A Lambda authorizer on Amazon API Gateway verifies the Amazon Cognito JWT and calls IsAuthorized for each of the caller’s groups. If no group is allowed, or Verified Permissions returns an error, the caller gets HTTP 403. Layer 2, document access. A middleware Lambda asks Verified Permissions which department knowledge bases the caller may query, and turns the answer into a metadata filter for RetrieveAndGenerate: equals for one department, orAll for several. The same policy store decides which model the caller may invoke. Output check. Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock checks that the answer is grounded in the retrieved context and filters harmful content. In the article’s example, dept-a and dept-b may query only their own documents and use Claude 3 Haiku, while dept-c may query every department and uses Amazon Nova Lite 2. Anything not permitted is denied by default, and a policy change applies on the next request without redeploying any code.
3. How a request flows graph LR U[User with Cognito JWT] --> W[CloudFront and AWS WAF] W --> G[API Gateway] G -- Layer 1 --> A[Lambda authorizer] A -- IsAuthorized --> P[Verified Permissions] G --> M[Middleware Lambda] M -- Layer 2 --> P M -- metadata filter --> K[Bedrock Knowledge Base] K --> R[Guardrails] R --> O[Grounded answer] AWS WAF applies rate limits and rules. If it denies, the request is blocked. Lambda authorizer (Layer 1) checks whether the caller may invoke the API. If not, the answer is 403. Middleware (Layer 2) works out which departments the caller may read. If none, the result is empty. Bedrock Knowledge Bases applies the metadata filter before the vector search, so the model never sees an unauthorized document. Guardrails checks that the answer is grounded. If not, it is blocked or modified. 4. Tagging documents at ingestion A file uploaded to S3 under a department prefix (for example docs/dept-a/report.pdf) triggers an EventBridge event, which is queued in SQS. A Lambda function writes a .metadata.json sidecar next to the file, {"metadataAttributes": {"department": "dept-a"}}. Failed attempts go to a dead-letter queue. Every five minutes a scheduled Lambda calls StartIngestionJob. Bedrock chunks the documents (300 tokens with 20% overlap), embeds them and indexes them together with their department attribute. A document without a sidecar is skipped and logged, so an untagged file never becomes visible to everyone. 5. Safe deployment checklist Know the isolation level. This is filter-level (logical) isolation, not isolation enforced by IAM or separate infrastructure. For different customers of a SaaS product, the article recommends one knowledge base per tenant. Fail closed. Both layers deny when Verified Permissions is unavailable. Caching the last known decisions would improve availability, but could keep honouring revoked access. Keep the authorizer cache short. The API Gateway default of 300 seconds can keep revoked access alive for up to five minutes. A TTL of 0 or 30–60 seconds revokes faster, at the cost of more Verified Permissions calls. Protect the policies and the tags. Restrict who can create, update or delete policies, log every change with CloudTrail, and let only the tagging Lambda write sidecar files. S3 Versioning and Object Lock help here. Mind the ingestion window. There is a short gap between an upload and its sidecar. The SQS batching window (30 seconds by default) should fit the ingestion schedule. Guardrails are not a complete defence against prompt injection, so input length checks and query sanitization are still needed. Personal view What I like most in this pattern is that authorization becomes data instead of code. Adding a department takes a Cedar policy, a Cognito group and tagged documents, with no new infrastructure.
The AI service of Fitness Assistant already does retrieval-augmented generation with Amazon Bedrock and a vector index on OpenSearch Serverless (see Workshop 5.4.8 and 5.4.9). Its index is filled by scheduled jobs from shared sources such as PubMed, RSS feeds and web articles. Access is controlled per function with IAM: each Lambda role may invoke only the Bedrock models it needs, and the AI routes are throttled in API Gateway. The article’s pattern becomes useful as soon as private documents enter that index, for example a gym’s internal material that only its own trainers and members should see. A Cedar policy per gym and a gym_id metadata attribute would then fit better than one index per gym.
Conclusion The pattern combines three ideas: one shared knowledge base with metadata, Cedar policies that live outside the code and change at runtime, and two independent layers that both fail closed. It is a cost-effective way to give each department its own view of shared data, as long as the team remembers that the isolation is logical and protects the policies and tags as carefully as the documents themselves.
References AWS Architecture Blog: Secure multi-tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock and Verified Permissions Amazon Verified Permissions documentation Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation Cedar policy language

title: 5.2.4 AWS Services and Selection Rationale
content: AWS Service Used for Why this, not an alternative AWS Lambda Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment and AI — 12 long-lived functions (HTTP, jobs, AI Worker) plus migration functions Six of seven services are short request/response or scheduled work with no need to hold a connection open. Lambda scales to zero between requests — important for a DEV environment that is idle most of the time — and removes the instance-sizing problem this project had already hit with a self-hosted model on EC2 (see Week 8). Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate Chat Service (REST + Socket.IO), and the one-shot database migrator task The one service that cannot be Lambda: Socket.IO holds a persistent connection per session. Fargate runs the container without any server to patch; dev sizing is 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB. The same cluster runs the data-migration task on demand. Amazon ECR Images for the Chat Service and the database migrator Private registry in the same region, pulled by ECS through the task execution role — no Docker Hub credentials or rate limits. Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Single entry point for the six Lambda services and the Chat REST routes One routing layer with explicit route prefixes instead of one public endpoint per service; HTTP API is cheaper than REST API and supports per-route throttling, used to protect Bedrock cost. Elastic Load Balancing (ALB) Front door for the Chat Fargate task Handles Socket.IO/WebSocket upgrades, health checks on /health, stickiness and path rules that hide /internal/* and /metrics. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 One cluster, seven logical databases Managed PostgreSQL that matches the application’s Prisma schemas, scales capacity (ACU) automatically and can drop to a low floor (0.5 ACU during deployment, 0 when idle). One cluster instead of seven keeps cost and operations down while each service keeps its own database and secret. Amazon Bedrock Chat and vision (Nova Pro via the APAC inference profile) and embeddings (Cohere Embed Multilingual v3) Replaces the self-hosted Ollama model: no instance to size, no API key to manage (IAM only), billed per token, reached from the VPC like any AWS API. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless Vector search for RAG and knowledge retrieval (fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors) Replaces the self-hosted Qdrant container: k-NN (FAISS/HNSW, 1024 dimensions) without servers, private through a VPC endpoint, IAM + data-access-policy authorization, and the NextGen collection group scales between 0 and 2 OCU. Amazon SQS AI task queue and its dead-letter queue Decouples long AI generations from the 30-second HTTP path; the Worker processes one message at a time and failed messages land in the DLQ after two attempts. Replaces Redis/BullMQ, which would have needed a running cache cluster. Amazon EventBridge Scheduler 13 schedules for settlements, reminders, payouts, reconciliation and AI jobs Managed cron per job with retries, without a long-running process or setInterval inside an HTTP function. Amazon S3 Static frontend; private uploads (profile photos, PT documents, contracts); deployment artifacts; migration dumps Four buckets with four different access models — public-read website, private with presigned URLs, private artifacts for Lambda, private versioned dumps — so data never shares a bucket with public assets. AWS Secrets Manager Every database credential, the database URL for Chat, the shared internal secret No password in code, images or plain environment variables; each function holds only a secret ID and resolves it at runtime. AWS IAM One role per function or task, scoped to its own secret, queue, model and invoke targets Least privilege per service instead of a broad shared role — see 5.2.5. Amazon VPC, NAT Gateway, Internet Gateway, VPC endpoints Network isolation and controlled egress Lambda, Fargate and Aurora sit in private subnets; one NAT Gateway gives outbound access (Bedrock); interface endpoints keep Secrets Manager and OpenSearch traffic inside the VPC; DB subnets have no internet route at all. Amazon CloudWatch Logs Logs for every Lambda, the Chat task and the migrator Default destination for both compute types; used for troubleshooting during deployment. Alarms are an open item (5.2.6). Deliberately not used (yet) Amazon CloudFront — planned once the frontend moves off the plain S3 website endpoint, so the bucket can become private behind Origin Access Control and the site can use HTTPS. Not usable in this account yet. AWS WAF — there is no CloudFront distribution or HTTPS listener to attach a web ACL to at this stage. Amazon ElastiCache — not needed: queues moved to SQS and the Chat Service runs a single task. It becomes necessary only to share Socket.IO state across several Chat tasks. CI/CD (CodePipeline/CodeBuild or GitHub Actions) — every deployment so far was a manual, documented console/CLI step; this is the largest remaining gap.

title: 5.4 Deployment Guide
content:
The services were deployed one at a time, in dependency order: each service only goes live after every service it calls is already running. The pages below follow that order and keep the screenshots captured during the real deployment.
5.4.1 Shared network infrastructure — Internet Gateway, public subnets, NAT Gateway and route tables. 5.4.2 Auth Service and API Gateway — the first Lambda, the HTTP API and its explicit public routes. 5.4.3 Frontend on Amazon S3 — static website hosting and the redeploy procedure. 5.4.4 User Service — Lambda-to-Lambda calls, private S3 uploads and the first scheduled jobs. 5.4.5 Fitness Service — migration from an S3 artifact and two reminder schedules. 5.4.6 Gym Service — QR check-in secret and payout/referral jobs. 5.4.7 Payment Service — VNPAY configuration, reconciliation and the Gym ↔ Payment wiring. 5.4.8 AI Service — database, queue and Bedrock — HTTP Lambda, SQS worker and jobs Lambda on Nova Pro / Cohere. 5.4.9 AI Service — vector search, scheduling and API — OpenSearch Serverless, knowledge ingestion, routes and rate limits. 5.4.10 Chat Service on ECS Fargate — container image, task definition, ALB and Socket.IO. 5.4.11 Data migration to Aurora — restoring 7 local databases with a one-shot Fargate task. The pattern every Lambda-based service follows Once the shared network exists, each service (Auth, User, Fitness, Gym, Payment, AI) is deployed with the same sequence. The service pages only call out what differs.
# Step Detail 1 Database secret Secrets Manager → Other type of secret with username, password, host, port, database = fitness_assistant_<service>, named fitness-assistant/dev/<service>-database. Rotation off for DEV. 2 Migration role IAM role trusted by Lambda with AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole + AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole, plus an inline policy allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on only that service’s secret ARN. 3 Migration Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-migrate, Node.js 22.x, x86_64, 1024 MB, handler dist/migrate-lambda.handler, env DATABASE_SECRET_ID, attached to both private app subnets and fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg. Invoked once with {}: it creates the logical database if missing and runs prisma migrate deploy, refusing to run against any other database name. 4 Runtime role Same two managed policies, plus inline policies for the service’s own secret and lambda:InvokeFunction on the exact functions it calls. 5 HTTP Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-<service>, 1024 MB, 30 s timeout, handler dist/lambda.handler, same VPC settings. 6 API Gateway Lambda integration (payload format 2.0) and explicit route prefixes. /internal/* and ANY /{proxy+} are never created. 7 Jobs Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-jobs, same ZIP, handler dist/jobs-lambda.handler, 1 minute timeout. 8 Scheduler A dedicated role trusted by scheduler.amazonaws.com that can only invoke that jobs Lambda, and one EventBridge schedule per job with a {"job": "<name>"} payload. All screenshots on these pages come from the deployment runbook. Screens that originally showed a secret value (database master password, INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET) were redacted at pixel level before being included — the black boxes are intentional.

title: 5.4.4 User Service
content:
After login, the frontend immediately needs the user profile, onboarding and body profile, so the User Service came next. It introduced three patterns reused by later services: calling another Lambda directly instead of through the public API, private S3 uploads with presigned URLs, and scheduled jobs on EventBridge Scheduler.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_user Secret fitness-assistant/dev/user-database Functions fitness-assistant-dev-user (HTTP), fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs (jobs) Uploads bucket fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id> (private) Step 1 — Create the database secret Secrets Manager → Store a new secret → Other type of secret with username, password (the Aurora master password, taken directly from Secrets Manager), host (Aurora cluster endpoint), port = 5432 and database = fitness_assistant_user. Name it fitness-assistant/dev/user-database, rotation off.
Step 2 — Create the execution role IAM → Roles → Create role, trusted entity AWS service → Lambda, managed policies AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole only — not AdministratorAccess, AmazonRDSFullAccess, SecretsManagerReadWrite or AmazonS3FullAccess. Name: fitness-assistant-dev-user-lambda-role.
Step 3 — Allow the role to read only its own secret Role → Permissions → Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON, replacing SECRET_ARN with the full ARN copied from the secret’s page. "Resource": "*" is not acceptable.
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "secretsmanager:DescribeSecret"], "Resource": "SECRET_ARN" } ] } The schema was then migrated with a temporary fitness-assistant-dev-user-migrate Lambda using the common pattern. Then configure:

Step 6 — Upload the code Code → Upload from → .zip file: backend/services/user-service/artifacts/user-lambda.zip, then Runtime settings → Edit → Handler dist/lambda.handler.
Step 7 — Add the API Gateway integration API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Integrations → Manage integrations → Create: Lambda function fitness-assistant-dev-user, payload format 2.0. API Gateway adds the invoke permission on the function when the console asks.
Step 8 — Create greedy routes per prefix The User Service exposes more than 100 endpoints, so instead of creating each route by hand, one greedy route is created per public prefix and attached to the User integration:
GET /health ANY /profile/{proxy+} ANY /inbody/{proxy+} ANY /pt-applications/{proxy+} ANY /contracts/{proxy+} ANY /notifications/{proxy+} ANY /sessions/{proxy+} ANY /availability/{proxy+} ANY /admin/{proxy+} ANY /locations/{proxy+} ANY /pt/{proxy+} ANY /me/{proxy+} ANY /{proxy+} and ANY /internal/{proxy+} are never created — /internal/* is service-to-service only. /webhooks/dropbox-sign is also skipped because it is disabled while REQUIRE_CONTRACT_ESIGN=false.
A route that exists but has no integration attached returns {"message":"Not Found"}. After creating routes, always open Integrations → Attach integrations to routes and check that every route has a target.
Step 9 — Call Auth directly with Lambda Invoke Some User flows call /auth/internal/*, which is intentionally not public. Instead of exposing it, the User Lambda invokes the Auth Lambda directly. Add an inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-user-invoke-auth:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "InvokeAuthLambda", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth" } ] } Then add AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME = fitness-assistant-dev-auth to the User Lambda’s environment (keeping AUTH_SERVICE_URL for now).
Step 10 — Final S3 permissions and CORS for presigned uploads Profile photos, PT application documents and contract PDFs all live in the private uploads bucket. The inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-user-profile-upload is replaced with three statements, each limited to one prefix:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "UserProfilePhotos", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id>/profile-photos/*" }, { "Sid": "PTApplicationDocuments", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id>/pt-applications/*" }, { "Sid": "ContractDocuments", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-uploads-dev-<account-id>/contracts/*" } ] } No s3:*, no s3:ListBucket. The browser uploads directly to S3 with a presigned URL, so the uploads bucket gets a CORS rule (Permissions → Cross-origin resource sharing) while staying private:
[ { "AllowedOrigins": ["http://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>.s3-website-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com"], "AllowedMethods": ["PUT", "GET", "HEAD"], "AllowedHeaders": ["content-type", "x-amz-*"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"], "MaxAgeSeconds": 300 } ] Step 11 — Create the jobs Lambda Background jobs run in a separate function so the HTTP Lambda never runs timers. Create fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs (Node.js 22.x, x86_64, role fitness-assistant-dev-user-lambda-role), with the same VPC settings, 1024 MB and a 1 minute timeout.
Upload the same user-lambda.zip and set the handler to dist/jobs-lambda.handler.
Environment: DATABASE_SECRET_ID, NODE_ENV, AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME, USER_UPLOAD_BUCKET, REQUIRE_CONTRACT_ESIGN=false and the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET.
Step 12 — Create the scheduler role IAM → Roles → Create role with a custom trust policy for EventBridge Scheduler:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "scheduler.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] } Name it fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs-scheduler-role and add an inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-user-jobs that allows lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs only. The scheduler never reuses a Lambda execution role and never gets lambda:*.
Step 13 — Create the three schedules Amazon EventBridge → Scheduler → Schedules → Create schedule, one per job, each sending {"job": "<name>"} to fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs:
Schedule Rate Payload fitness-assistant-dev-user-session-settlement rate(5 minutes) {"job": "session-settlement"} fitness-assistant-dev-user-session-auto-confirm rate(10 minutes) {"job": "session-auto-confirm"} fitness-assistant-dev-user-reschedule-expiry rate(10 minutes) {"job": "reschedule-expiry"} Common settings: recurring rate-based schedule in the Asia/Saigon (UTC+07:00) time zone, flexible time window off, state enabled, action after completion NONE, retry enabled with maximum event age 5 minutes and 2 retry attempts, no DLQ for DEV, AWS-owned encryption key, and Use existing role → fitness-assistant-dev-user-jobs-scheduler-role (not Create new role).

title: Blog 4: Limit AWS Management Console Access to Trusted Networks
content:
Limit AWS Management Console Access to Trusted Networks with Sign-in Policies and RCPs Status: Draft — not yet shared externally.
Original article: Restrict AWS Management Console access to expected networks with sign-in resource-based policies and RCPs (AWS Security Blog, 24 June 2026)
For most teams, the AWS Management Console is the most powerful door into an AWS account: whoever signs in can see and change almost everything their permissions allow. A password and MFA prove who the user is, but not where the request comes from. In June 2026, AWS Sign-In gained resource-based policies and resource control policies (RCPs), so an account, or a whole organization, can refuse console sign-in from networks it does not expect. A post on the AWS Security Blog walks through this new control.
1. Why restricting sign-in by network used to be hard IAM and SCP conditions act after sign-in. A condition such as aws:SourceIp in an IAM policy or an SCP can deny API actions from unknown networks, but the user can still sign in and open the console. Identity provider rules cover only federated users. Network rules in an external identity provider do not apply to IAM users or to the root user. No single place to enforce it. Each account and each type of identity needed its own workaround. 2. The new control: sign-in policies and RCPs Sign-in resource-based policy, for one account. You describe the expected networks with a few parameters (a source IP range, a source VPC and its Region, and an excluded principal), and AWS Sign-In generates the policy: deny statements that block sign-in unless the request comes from an expected network or from the excluded principal. Resource control policy, for many accounts. The same rules, attached in AWS Organizations to the organization, an organizational unit or a single account, and applied automatically to every account in scope. A switch to turn it on. The statements have no effect until console authorization is enabled for the account, so they can be reviewed before they are enforced. The controls cost nothing extra and are available in all AWS commercial Regions. They do not replace IAM identity-based policies, which still decide what a signed-in user may do.
3. How a sign-in request is checked graph LR S[Sign-in request] --> N{Expected network or excluded principal} N -- no --> D[Denied and logged in CloudTrail] N -- yes --> A[Password and MFA] A --> T[Console session tokens] T -- checked again on refresh --> N T --> I[IAM policies decide each action] Before the credentials are checked, AWS Sign-In evaluates the signin:Authenticate action against the policy. A request from outside the expected IP range or VPC is denied, even with the correct password and MFA, unless it comes from the excluded principal. Normal authentication follows: password and MFA, or a federated sign-in. When the console asks for session tokens (signin:CreateOAuth2Token and signin:AuthorizeOAuth2Access), the same network rules are evaluated again, and again every time the session requests new credentials. Region binding stops a request that claims the allowed VPC but asks for another Region, because a VPC ID is only unique within one Region. Every attempt is logged as a ConsoleLogin event in CloudTrail. A blocked attempt shows AccessDenied with “Authorization denied because of a resource-based policy”, or “…resource control policy” when an RCP blocked it. 4. Safe deployment checklist List the expected networks first: the office and VPN egress IP ranges, and the VPC IDs (with their Regions) that users sign in from. Always keep an excluded principal for break-glass access, so a wrong range cannot lock everyone out. Create, review, then enable. Create the statements (write operations go to us-east-1), review them with aws signin get-resource-policy, and only then run aws signin put-console-authorization-configuration. Know the rollback: delete-console-authorization-configuration turns enforcement off, and delete-resource-permission-statement removes a statement. Start with a test account, then move to RCPs at the organization or OU level when many accounts need the same rule. Monitor CloudTrail for ConsoleLogin failures caused by the sign-in policy, to catch attacks as well as legitimate users on a new network. Combine it with Console Private Access and VPC endpoint policies to build a full network, identity and resource perimeter. Personal view What I like about this control is that it moves the check to the very first step. An attacker who phishes both a password and an MFA code still cannot use them from an unexpected network.
The DEV environment of Fitness Assistant was built mostly through the AWS Management Console (see Workshop 5.4), so console sign-in is the most powerful way into that account. MFA already protects it, but this project has no fixed office network. Before turning on a sign-in policy, I would first need a stable source address, such as a VPN with a fixed egress IP or a VPC reached through Console Private Access, plus an excluded break-glass principal, so that a new home IP address cannot lock me out of my own account.
Conclusion Sign-in resource-based policies and RCPs close a gap that IAM policies could not: they decide whether a console session may start at all, based on where the request comes from. They are generated from a few parameters, reviewed before they are enforced, logged in CloudTrail and free of charge. That makes them an easy extra layer for any account managed through the console, as long as an excluded principal keeps a safe way back in.
References AWS Security Blog: Restrict AWS Management Console access to expected networks with sign-in resource-based policies and RCPs AWS Sign-In User Guide: console access control AWS Organizations: resource control policies Data perimeter policy examples (aws-samples)

content:
WEEK 4 WORKLOG Week 4 Objectives: Complete self-study of Module 3: Optimizing the system Deepen understanding across the Operate, Security, and Reliability pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework Turn the module’s lessons into concrete requirements for the Fitness Assistant’s AWS design Start the AWS deployment: shared network, Aurora, the Auth service behind API Gateway, the frontend on S3 and the User service Tasks to be carried out this week: Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Materials Study and complete Module 3: Optimizing the system 24-8-2026 29-8-2026 Operate: 22: https://000022.awsstudygroup.com/ 27: https://000027.awsstudygroup.com/ 29: https://000029.awsstudygroup.com/ 31: https://000031.awsstudygroup.com/ 58: https://000058.awsstudygroup.com/ Security: 18: https://000018.awsstudygroup.com/ 26: https://000026.awsstudygroup.com/ 30: https://000030.awsstudygroup.com/ 33: https://000033.awsstudygroup.com/ 44: https://000044.awsstudygroup.com/ Reliability: 13: https://000013.awsstudygroup.com/ 19: https://000019.awsstudygroup.com/ 20: https://000020.awsstudygroup.com/ Deploy the shared network (VPC, subnets, NAT Gateway, security groups), Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2, the Auth service on Lambda behind API Gateway, and the frontend on S3 26-8-2026 27-8-2026 5.4.1 Shared network 5.4.2 Auth Service and API Gateway 5.4.3 Frontend on S3 Deploy the User service (database, Lambda functions and schedules) 27-8-2026 27-8-2026 5.4.4 User Service Week 4 Achievements: Overview:
During this week, I focused on system optimization (Module 3) by exploring three crucial pillars: Operations, Security, and Reliability. Besides the labs, I used each pillar as a checklist for the Fitness Assistant: what its AWS design must guarantee for access control, private networking, secrets, backups and monitoring, and what it would still cost while nobody is using it. The deployment itself also started this week: the shared network, Aurora, the Auth service behind API Gateway and the frontend on S3 on 26–27 August, then the User service on 27 August.
Learned theory:
Operations (Operate): Mastered programmatic cost optimization for EC2 instances using AWS Lambda, resource management through Tagging and Resource Groups, system monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch and visualization with Grafana, and centralized server management utilizing AWS Systems Manager.
Security: Deepened my understanding of access restrictions using IAM Permission Boundaries and condition keys. Explored threat detection with AWS Security Hub, web traffic filtering with AWS WAF, and data encryption strategies at rest (AWS KMS).
Reliability: Studied enterprise-grade network interconnectivity using VPC Peering and AWS Transit Gateway, alongside automated data retention utilizing AWS Backup.
Hands-on labs:
Operate:
Configured Lambda function to automatically start/stop EC2 instances on schedule (reduce costs when dev environment not in use) Set up CloudWatch dashboards for the lab resources Practised resource tagging and Resource Groups to find resources by environment and service Tested Systems Manager Session Manager for EC2 access without SSH keys Security:
Implemented IAM Permission Boundaries to limit developer user permissions Configured Security Groups with least privilege principle (only open necessary ports) Researched AWS WAF rules to protect API endpoints from common attacks (SQL injection, XSS) Studied KMS encryption at rest for databases and S3 buckets Reliability:
Designed a backup plan with AWS Backup (daily snapshots, 7-day retention) Researched multi-AZ deployment for production environment (ensuring high availability) Evaluated VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway for future microservices expansion Applied to Fitness Assistant:
Cost: The lab saves money by stopping idle EC2 instances on a schedule. For this project I took the idea one step further: use compute that costs nothing while idle (Lambda for the HTTP services and jobs, Aurora Serverless v2 with a low capacity floor), so there is nothing to stop. What still costs money when idle (NAT Gateway, load balancer, VPC endpoints) became the “sleep mode” in the budget. Security requirements (applied from the Auth service onward): one IAM role per function, scoped to its own secret, queue and model; database credentials in Secrets Manager, one secret per service database; compute and database only in private subnets; security groups that reference each other instead of IP ranges. Reliability requirements: private subnets in two Availability Zones, Aurora automated backups, load-balancer health checks that replace an unhealthy container, and a dead-letter queue so a failing background job is not retried forever. Monitoring plan: CloudWatch Logs for every function and task from day one, then alarms on the few signals that matter: function errors and throttles, dead-letter queue depth, database capacity and the chat target’s health. Difficulties Encountered: IAM Permission Boundaries complexity: The concept of Permission Boundaries (maximum permission limits) vs inline policies was quite confusing initially. Took considerable time to understand real-world use cases.
Cost optimization trade-offs: When researching Lambda-based EC2 scheduling, realized there are trade-offs between cost savings and developer convenience. Stopping dev instances might cause inconvenience if developers need to work outside regular hours.
Monitoring overhead: Setting up comprehensive monitoring requires upfront effort (define metrics, create dashboards, configure alarms). Need to balance between “monitor everything” vs “monitor what matters”.
How It Was Resolved: Permission Boundaries: Drew diagrams to visualize relationships between identity-based policies, permission boundaries, and resource-based policies. Practiced with concrete examples in labs.
Cost optimization: Avoided the trade-off instead of tuning a schedule: services that scale to zero need no stop/start at all, and the few fixed-cost resources are paused on purpose between test sessions (see 5.7 Clean-up).
Monitoring strategy: Adopted “start simple, iterate” approach: logs first (Lambda functions and ECS tasks send them to CloudWatch with almost no setup), then a short list of alarms on the signals above. The EC2 host metrics used in the lab (CPU, memory, disk) do not apply, because a serverless design has no host to watch.
AWS Skills / Services Learned: Services:
AWS Lambda (event-driven automation) Amazon CloudWatch (logs, metrics, alarms) AWS Systems Manager (Session Manager, Patch Manager) AWS IAM (Permission Boundaries, condition keys) AWS Security Hub (security posture management) AWS WAF (web application firewall) AWS KMS (encryption key management) AWS Backup (automated backup orchestration) VPC Peering and AWS Transit Gateway (network connectivity) Skills:
Cost optimization strategies for cloud infrastructure Security best practices (least privilege, defense in depth) Centralized monitoring and observability Infrastructure automation with Lambda Backup and disaster recovery planning Connection to Fitness Assistant Architecture: Module 3 insights directly applicable:
Operate: CloudWatch Logs for every Lambda function and the chat task; alarms on errors, throttles, dead-letter queue depth and database capacity (planned) Security: least-privilege role per function, credentials in Secrets Manager, KMS encryption for user data; AWS WAF cannot be attached to an API Gateway HTTP API directly, so it is planned together with CloudFront Reliability: private subnets in two AZs, Aurora automated backups, health checks with automatic task replacement, dead-letter queue for failed jobs Related Workshop Sections: 5.2.5 Security and IAM - Network isolation, least-privilege roles and secrets 5.2.6 Scalability and Operations - Operations, logging and monitoring

title: 5.2.5 Security and IAM
content:
Network isolation Lambda functions and the Chat Fargate task run only in the two private application subnets; the only resources in public subnets are the NAT Gateway and the internet-facing Chat ALB. Aurora sits in private DB subnets whose route table has no NAT or internet route, so the database tier can neither reach nor be reached from the internet. Security groups reference each other instead of IP ranges: Security group Inbound fitness-assistant-dev-aurora-sg 5432 from lambda-sg and from chat-sg only fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg 3005 from chat-alb-sg only fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg 80 from the internet (DEV, HTTP) fitness-assistant-dev-vpce-sg 443 from lambda-sg (Secrets Manager and OpenSearch endpoints) fitness-assistant-dev-lambda-sg none OpenSearch Serverless is reachable only through its VPC endpoint (public access disabled). The Chat ALB answers /internal/* and /metrics with a fixed 404, and API Gateway has no /internal/*, /metrics or catch-all route, so service-to-service endpoints are not reachable from the internet at all. IAM — least privilege per function Every function and task has its own role. Lambda roles start from AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole (logs) and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole (VPC networking) and add inline policies that name exact resources:
Need How it is scoped Database credentials secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on that service’s own secret ARN only Calling another service lambda:InvokeFunction on the exact target function ARNs (e.g. Payment → Auth, User, Gym, AI), never lambda:* Private uploads s3:PutObject/GetObject/DeleteObject on three prefixes of the uploads bucket only (profile-photos/, pt-applications/, contracts/), no s3:ListBucket AI queue HTTP Lambda: sqs:SendMessage; Worker: ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage, GetQueueAttributes — on the one queue Bedrock bedrock:InvokeModel on the APAC Nova Pro inference profile, on the Nova Pro foundation model only when called through that profile (IAM condition), and on Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 — no AmazonBedrockFullAccess, no streaming permission OpenSearch aoss:APIAccessAll on the one collection ARN, plus a data access policy that grants index read/write/create to the three AI roles but not DeleteIndex Schedules One scheduler role per service, trusted by scheduler.amazonaws.com, allowed to invoke only that service’s jobs function ECS Execution role (pull image, write logs, inject the two Chat secrets) separated from the task role (invoke Auth/User only) Migration task Read only the dumps prefix of the migration bucket and the database credential The Cohere Marketplace subscription was accepted once by an administrator; runtime roles have no aws-marketplace:* permission.
Secrets All database credentials are in AWS Secrets Manager, one secret per service database (fitness-assistant/dev/<service>-database); functions hold only DATABASE_SECRET_ID. The Chat task receives its database URL and the internal secret as ECS secrets (valueFrom), never as plain values. Service-to-service calls carry the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, separate from any user JWT. The Gym Service signs QR check-in codes with its own CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET, deliberately different from the internal secret. Payment provider keys are entered only once real sandbox credentials exist and are never copied into chat, documentation or source control. Bedrock needs no API key — every model call is authorized by the function’s IAM role. Abuse and cost protection API Gateway route throttling on the AI routes (1 request/s with a burst of 3; 3/6 for the marketplace) caps how fast any client can trigger billable Bedrock calls; the frontend shows a “too many requests” message on HTTP 429. SQS dead-letter queue (2 attempts) prevents a failing AI job from being retried forever. Known gaps (open, not hidden) Internal secrets in Lambda configuration — INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET and CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET are Lambda environment variables (encrypted at rest, but readable by anyone allowed to view the function configuration). Chat already reads the internal secret from Secrets Manager; moving the Lambda copies there is a hardening follow-up. HTTPS — the S3 website endpoint and the Chat ALB are HTTP-only in DEV; HTTPS needs a domain and an ACM certificate, ideally with CloudFront in front of a private bucket (Origin Access Control). Public-read frontend bucket — temporary, objects only (s3:GetObject), until CloudFront is available. No WAF yet — nothing to attach a web ACL to until CloudFront or an HTTPS listener exists. ADMIN credential rotation and 12 remaining seed accounts — postponed, required before any wider release. Screenshot evidence that contained secrets A few console screenshots in the deployment runbook (Secrets Manager “Store a new secret” screens and Lambda “Environment variables” screens) originally showed real secret values. Each was redacted at pixel level — the value itself blacked out in the image data, not cropped or blurred — before being included in this report; the black boxes in 5.4 are intentional. All screenshots were reviewed again before publication.

During this intensive week, I accomplished two major tracks: system performance/cost optimization (Module 3) and application modernization (Module 4). The extensive lab workload spanned containerization, robust serverless computing, data lakes, and complex cost analytics. Module 4 also explained the pattern the deployment had followed since Week 4 (most of the Fitness Assistant does not need servers at all), and I applied it to the Fitness service on 2 September.
Note: Certain sections within the modernization labs (specifically 47, 54, and 55) mandated the use of AWS Cloud9. As AWS Cloud9 is currently inaccessible in my environment, these specific sections were strategically skipped, while the underlying architectural concepts were still thoroughly studied.
Learned theory:
Performance & Cost Optimization: Learned deployment paradigms using Docker and Amazon ECS. Mastered CI/CD automation with AWS CodePipeline. Studied Data Lake foundations and explored financial governance via Savings Plans, EC2 right-sizing, and AWS Glue/Athena querying.
Modernization & Microservices: Grasped architectural patterns for migrating monolithic applications to microservices. Explored decoupled messaging/eventing systems and integrating orchestration tools like AWS Step Functions.
Serverless Architecture: Deepened my expertise in the serverless ecosystem utilizing AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, the Serverless Application Model (SAM), Amazon Cognito for identity, SQS/SNS for asynchronous processing, and AppSync.
Hands-on labs:
Successfully deployed containerized applications on ECS, integrating them with automated CI/CD pipelines Configured enterprise storage solutions including File Storage Gateways and FSx for Windows, alongside Data Lake optimizations Executed advanced cost tracking and query analysis utilizing AWS Glue and Amazon Athena Engineered and deployed fully serverless applications (e.g., Serverless Bookstore), encompassing frontend API integration, SSL setup, CI/CD workflows, and CloudWatch/X-Ray distributed tracing Skipped specific execution steps in Labs 47, 54, and 55 due to an inability to provision AWS Cloud9 environments, though the theoretical framework for Step Functions, Messaging/Eventing, and SPA configurations was thoroughly reviewed Applied to Fitness Assistant:
Modernization Path (the pattern every service follows):
The application is already split into services (auth, user, fitness, gym, payment, ai, chat) that run together with Docker Compose locally. Six of them only answer short HTTP requests or run scheduled jobs, which is exactly the Lambda model; only chat has to keep a Socket.IO connection open. Each of the six HTTP services runs as Lambda functions behind one API Gateway HTTP API, which replaces the application gateway container as the single entry point (Auth and User since Week 4, Fitness this week). Scheduled work (session settlement, workout reminders, payouts, payment reconciliation, AI knowledge refresh) moves from timers inside the process to EventBridge Scheduler, which invokes one jobs function per service. Long AI work (workout and nutrition plan generation) moves to an SQS queue and a worker function, so no HTTP call has to wait past API Gateway’s ~30-second limit. This also replaces the Redis/BullMQ queue, which would have needed a cache cluster running all the time. Chat stays a container; where to run it is evaluated in Week 6. Performance Optimization:
Memory is the only sizing setting on Lambda (CPU grows with it), so there are no instance types to right-size Considered CloudFront CDN for frontend assets to reduce latency, postponed until the site has a domain and HTTPS Cost Optimization:
Pay-per-use services for the application tier (Lambda, HTTP API, which is cheaper than a REST API, SQS, EventBridge Scheduler) and Aurora Serverless v2 instead of a fixed-size database instance Listed the costs that remain while the app is idle (NAT Gateway, load balancer, VPC endpoints, the database’s capacity floor); they became the main lines of the budget One naming scheme for every resource (fitness-assistant-dev-<service>-…), so cost and clean-up can be filtered per service Researched Savings Plans for predictable workloads (Compute Savings Plans also cover Lambda and Fargate) Set up AWS Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection alerts CI/CD:
Sketched a pipeline: build each service’s Lambda package into the deployments bucket and the chat image into ECR, then update the functions and the ECS service. Not built yet: deployments are manual and documented step by step in 5.4, and CI/CD is the largest open item. Difficulties Encountered: Cloud9 Limitation: Unable to access AWS Cloud9 (possibly due to region restrictions or account limitations), resulting in skipped hands-on steps in labs 47, 54, 55. However, conceptual learning was maintained through documentation and video tutorials.
Mapping Docker Compose to serverless: In Docker Compose every service is a long-running container that calls the others by hostname. On Lambda there is no long-running process and no hostname, so in-process timers, the Redis queue and service-to-service calls all had to change.
Serverless Cold Start Trade-offs: When researching Lambda migration, realized cold start latency could impact user experience for synchronous APIs. Needed to carefully evaluate which workloads are suitable for serverless.
Cost Calculation Complexity: AWS cost model is very granular (per request, per GB-second, data transfer costs). Difficult to forecast costs accurately when planning serverless migration.
How It Was Resolved: Cloud9 Workaround: Used local development environment with AWS CLI and SAM CLI to simulate Cloud9 workflows. Read lab documentation thoroughly to understand intended outcomes.
Mapping: Listed every long-running part of each service and chose a managed replacement for each: timers → EventBridge Scheduler and a jobs function, Redis/BullMQ → SQS and a worker, sockets → the chat container on ECS, service-to-service HTTP calls → direct Lambda invocations on exact function ARNs.
Cold Start Mitigation: Accepted cold starts for the DEV environment, where they only affect the first request after an idle period. Provisioned concurrency remains the option for production, so the synchronous APIs did not need to stay on containers.
Cost Forecasting: Used AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs. Set up granular billing alerts. Deployed one service at a time (Auth and User in Week 4, Fitness this week), so the cost of each step could be checked.

title: Workshop
content:
Workshop — Deploying Gymini (Fitness Assistant) on AWS Serverless This workshop documents how the Fitness Assistant application (branded Gymini) was deployed to AWS as a serverless-first DEV environment in ap-southeast-1: six Lambda-based microservices behind Amazon API Gateway, one ECS Fargate service for real-time chat, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2, Amazon Bedrock for AI, and OpenSearch Serverless for vector search. Every step is reconstructed from the deployment runbook kept while the system was built, with the original console screenshots.
Contents 5.1 Overview 5.2 Architecture Description 5.3 Prerequisite 5.4 Deployment Guide 5.5 Test & Validation 5.6 Demo 5.7 Clean-up

title: 5.2.6 Scalability and Operations
content:
How each component scales Component Scaling model Notes Service Lambdas (HTTP and jobs) Per invocation, automatic, scale to zero 1024 MB each; cold starts on idle functions are the trade-off, not yet measured. No reserved concurrency, so one hot route cannot starve the others by configuration. AI Worker One Lambda per SQS message (batch size 1) Throughput grows with queue depth; failed messages go to the DLQ after 2 receives. Chat Service (ECS Fargate) Fixed at 1 task (0.5 vCPU / 1 GB) Deliberate: Socket.IO session state is in memory, so a second task would split sessions until a shared adapter (e.g. Redis) exists. No service auto scaling yet. Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 Capacity in ACUs between a floor and a ceiling Floor kept at 0.5 ACU during deployment so auto-pause/resume does not disturb smoke tests; can go to 0 when idle. OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) 0–2 OCU for indexing and for search Scales to zero after ~10 idle minutes; the first request afterwards can take 10–30 s. API Gateway, SQS, EventBridge, S3 Fully managed No capacity planning needed at DEV traffic. AI routes are intentionally throttled. Keeping slow work out of the request path Scheduled work runs from EventBridge Scheduler into dedicated jobs functions, so no user request ever triggers a settlement or reconciliation run. Long AI work goes through SQS to the AI Worker (300 s timeout) and knowledge ingestion runs in the AI Jobs function (600 s timeout), while the HTTP function stays under API Gateway’s ~30 s integration limit. That is why the AI Service has three functions instead of one.
Operating the system today Deployments are manual and documented step by step in 5.4: ZIPs uploaded from the deployments bucket, task definition revisions rolled out with Force new deployment, and schema changes applied with each service’s migration function. Logs for every function and task are in CloudWatch Logs (/aws/lambda/…, /ecs/…); 5.5.4 lists what to look for. Changing a secret (for example a rotated Aurora password) requires recycling the Lambda execution environments, because functions cache the secret while warm — the Auth deployment did this by editing a harmless DEPLOY_REVISION variable. Operational gaps, tracked openly No CI/CD yet — the largest remaining operational piece. No CloudWatch alarms yet — logs exist, but nothing pages on errors, throttles, DLQ messages, Aurora capacity or an unhealthy Chat target. End-to-end validation incomplete — Auth and User are verified; the remaining services are deployed but pending (5.5.5). Chat is a single task — acceptable for DEV, revisited before any real multi-user load. A serverless architecture that scales its compute automatically is not “production-ready” by itself; the missing pipeline, alarms and test coverage above are exactly what a purely architectural description could hide, so they are named here.

title: 5.4.6 Gym Service
content:
The Gym Service handles gyms, PT listings, owner and admin tools, collaborations and QR check-in. It is the first service with a second secret of its own: the key that signs check-in QR codes.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_gym (9 Prisma migrations) Secret fitness-assistant/dev/gym-database Functions fitness-assistant-dev-gym, fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs Calls Auth, User and (after 5.4.7) Payment Lambdas Step 1 — Create the database secret Same structure as the other services, with database = fitness_assistant_gym.
Step 2 — Upload the artifacts Upload gym-migrate-lambda.zip (~69 MiB, so S3 is mandatory) and gym-lambda.zip (~36 MiB — small enough for a direct upload, but S3 is used for consistency) to fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>.
At this point in the runbook the Gym migration was skipped, even though the service has 9 migrations: the Lambda and its routes can be deployed, but every route that touches the database fails until fitness_assistant_gym has its schema. The migration was run with a fitness-assistant-dev-gym-migrate function following the common pattern — it appears in the function list in 5.4.10 — and the deployment status table records the Gym migration as complete.
Step 3 — Create the runtime role fitness-assistant-dev-gym-lambda-role (AWS service → Lambda, the two managed policies), with two inline policies:
fitness-assistant-dev-gym-database-secret — secretsmanager:GetSecretValue / DescribeSecret on fitness-assistant/dev/gym-database*. fitness-assistant-dev-gym-service-invoke — lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-auth and fitness-assistant-dev-user. Payment is deliberately not in the invoke list yet — it is added in 5.4.7 once the Payment Lambda exists.
Step 4 — Create the Gym Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-gym, Node.js 22.x, x86_64, role fitness-assistant-dev-gym-lambda-role, 1024 MB, 30 s, handler dist/lambda.handler, code from s3://fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>/gym-lambda.zip (copy mode).
Step 5 — Environment variables Variable Value NODE_ENV production DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/gym-database AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME fitness-assistant-dev-auth USER_LAMBDA_NAME fitness-assistant-dev-user INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the shared service-to-service value CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET a new, strong random value CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET must be different from INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET: it signs the QR codes shown to gym members, so leaking one must not compromise the other. PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME and FITNESS_LAMBDA_NAME are not set yet.
Step 6 — Connect the Gym Lambda to API Gateway Create the Lambda integration fitness-assistant-dev-gym (payload 2.0), then the root + greedy route pair for each prefix:
ANY /gyms ANY /gyms/{proxy+} ANY /pt ANY /pt/{proxy+} ANY /me ANY /me/{proxy+} ANY /owner ANY /owner/{proxy+} ANY /admin ANY /admin/{proxy+} ANY /collaborations ANY /collaborations/{proxy+} /me, /admin and /pt can already exist from the User Service. An HTTP API cannot route the same method and path to two integrations, so when the console reports an existing route it is not overwritten — the conflict is resolved by checking which service’s code actually owns that path. The Payment Service later avoids the problem entirely by using more specific prefixes such as /me/wallet.
The API now routes:
fitness-assistant-dev-api ├── /auth/* → Auth Lambda ├── User routes → User Lambda ├── Fitness routes → Fitness Lambda └── Gym routes → Gym Lambda ──► Auth / User Lambda, Aurora (fitness_assistant_gym) Step 7 — Create the jobs Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs: same role and artifact, handler dist/jobs-lambda.handler, 1024 MB, 1 minute, same VPC and environment variables (including CHECKIN_TOKEN_SECRET).
Step 8 — Scheduler role and schedules Create fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs-scheduler-role (trust scheduler.amazonaws.com) with an inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-gym-jobs allowing lambda:InvokeFunction on the Gym jobs Lambda only, then two schedules:
Schedule Rate Payload fitness-assistant-dev-gym-membership-payout rate(10 minutes) {"job":"membership-payout-sweep"} fitness-assistant-dev-gym-referral-settlement rate(10 minutes) {"job":"referral-settlement-sweep"} Both: flexible window off, enabled, maximum event age 5 minutes, 2 retry attempts, no DLQ, AWS-owned key, the existing scheduler role. Both jobs need the Payment Service, which is why the Gym jobs Lambda also receives PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME in the next page.

title: 5.6 Demo
content:
The deployment runbook only contains AWS console evidence. Screenshots and a short screen recording of the running application are captured during the final end-to-end pass (5.5.5) and added to this page; until then the page describes the demo script, so the demo is reproducible by anyone with access to the DEV environment.
Entry points What URL Web application http://fitness-assistant-frontend-dev-<account-id>.s3-website-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com REST API https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com Real-time chat http://fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-<id>.ap-southeast-1.elb.amazonaws.com (used by the frontend for Socket.IO) 5.6.1 Member journey Register and log in — /register, verify, then /login (Auth Lambda, JWT). Onboarding and profile — body profile, goals, profile photo uploaded straight to the private S3 bucket with a presigned URL (User Lambda). Training — browse exercises, create or import a workout plan, start and finish a workout; the reminder jobs pick up today’s planned workouts (Fitness Lambda + EventBridge). AI coach — ask a question in the AI chat (Bedrock Nova Pro, grounded on the OpenSearch knowledge indexes), then request a generated workout or nutrition plan and watch it complete through the SQS worker (AI HTTP Lambda → SQS → AI Worker). Gyms and personal trainers — browse gyms and PTs, check in at a gym with the signed QR code (Gym Lambda). Payment — top up the wallet or pay for a PT contract through the VNPAY sandbox; the payment is confirmed by the provider callback and the 5-minute reconciliation job (Payment Lambda). Chat — open a conversation with a PT; messages arrive live over Socket.IO (Chat on ECS Fargate). 5.6.2 Admin journey Log in with an admin account. Users — list users, change a role, disable and re-enable an account (/auth/users/*). PT applications and contracts — review PT applications and their documents (User Lambda, private S3). Payments — review transactions and withdrawals (/admin/payments/*). AI administration — open the AI overview (/admin/ai/*), rate-limited like every AI route. What the demo proves Step AWS path exercised Any page load S3 static website Login, profile, training, gyms, payments, admin API Gateway → service Lambda → Aurora (private subnets) AI answers and plans API Gateway → AI Lambda → Bedrock (via NAT) and OpenSearch (via VPC endpoint), SQS → AI Worker Reminders, settlements, reconciliation EventBridge Scheduler → jobs Lambdas Live chat Chat ALB → ECS Fargate → Aurora Neither the AI coach nor any other feature of the application replaces medical advice.
