Container Strategy Evaluation:
By this week Auth, User and Fitness were running on Lambda (see Week 5), and Gym and Payment followed on 8 September. The question for this week was narrower: where should the one service that needs a long-running process run? That service is Chat, which keeps a Socket.IO connection open for every user. I compared the three platforms from the module:
Amazon Lightsail Containers:
Pros: Simple setup, predictable pricing ($10-40/month), good for MVP Cons: Limited scaling, and harder to integrate with the private VPC, per-service IAM roles and Secrets Manager used by the rest of the design Decision: Not used Amazon ECS with Fargate:
Pros: Serverless (no server management), good AWS integration, cost-effective for small-medium scale Cons: Vendor lock-in (AWS-specific), learning curve Decision: Chosen for the Chat service, deployed in Week 8. The same cluster can also run one-off tasks, later used for the database migration job Amazon EKS (Kubernetes):
Pros: Industry standard, portable, powerful orchestration Cons: Complex setup, a control-plane fee for every cluster, overkill for a single container service Decision: Not needed at this scale Implementation Plan for the Chat Service:
Phase 1 - Image and registry:
Build the production image of chat-service for linux/amd64 Push it to a private Amazon ECR repository in the same region Phase 2 - Task and service:
One task definition: 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, container port 3005, database URL and internal secret injected from Secrets Manager One ECS service with the Fargate launch type in the private application subnets Phase 3 - Load balancer and routing:
Internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the public subnets, with an IP target group checked on /health Target-group stickiness and a longer idle timeout, so Socket.IO connections are not cut Listener rules that answer /internal/* and /metrics with 404; REST calls under /chat/* reach the ALB through API Gateway Later:
Run more than one Chat task only after adding a shared Socket.IO adapter (session state is kept in memory today) CI/CD for the image; CloudWatch Container Insights and an alarm on target health Architecture Comparison:
First plan (lift-and-shift onto one host):
User → EC2 (Docker Compose with all services, Ollama, Qdrant, Redis) → RDS Chosen design:
Browser → S3 static website (frontend) Browser → API Gateway (HTTP API) → Lambda (auth, user, fitness, gym, payment, ai) → Aurora PostgreSQL Browser → Chat ALB (Socket.IO; REST through API Gateway /chat/*) → ECS Fargate (chat) → Aurora PostgreSQL Difficulties Encountered: ECS vs EKS Decision: Initially confused about when to use ECS vs EKS. ECS simpler but AWS-specific, EKS industry standard but much more complex.
Task Definition Complexity: ECS Task Definitions have many configuration options (CPU, memory, networking mode, volume mounts, environment variables, secrets). Hard to optimize correctly.
Fargate Pricing Model: Fargate pricing based on vCPU and memory allocated per second, and the load balancer in front of it is a fixed monthly cost. At DEV traffic, the always-on chat path costs more than all six Lambda services together.
Service-to-service calls: In Docker Compose the services call each other by hostname on a shared network. Neither Lambda functions nor a Fargate task behind a load balancer have that, and AWS Cloud Map for service discovery has its own learning curve.
How It Was Resolved: Platform Decision: ECS on Fargate for Chat only: production-ready, AWS-integrated, manageable complexity, lower cost than EKS. EKS stays an option if the project ever needs Kubernetes or multi-cloud portability.
Task Definitions: Started from the smallest task definition that works (one container, one port, secrets from Secrets Manager) and kept every change as a new revision.
Cost Management: Used AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate Fargate and ALB costs. Kept Chat at one small task that can be scaled to zero between test sessions; Savings Plans only if a steady baseline appears.
Service-to-service calls: No Cloud Map: internal calls are direct Lambda invocations on exact function ARNs that carry a shared internal secret, and the chat task calls Auth and User the same way. API Gateway has no /internal/* route, so these endpoints are never public.
AWS Skills / Services Learned: Services:
Amazon Lightsail Containers Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) AWS Fargate (serverless compute for containers) Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) AWS CodePipeline (for container CI/CD) Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry) AWS Cloud Map (service discovery) Application Load Balancer (ALB) AWS Copilot CLI Skills:
Container orchestration strategies ECS vs EKS evaluation and selection Fargate serverless container management Kubernetes fundamentals (EKS) CI/CD pipeline design for containers Microservices deployment patterns Service discovery and inter-service communication Container cost optimization Connection to Fitness Assistant Architecture: Immediate Actions:
Production Dockerfile for chat-service (the other services are packaged as Lambda ZIP files instead of images) One task definition and one ECS service for Chat ALB rules for Socket.IO and for hiding internal paths Medium-term Goals:
Implement full CI/CD pipeline Shared Socket.IO adapter before scaling Chat beyond one task Alarm on the chat target’s health Related Workshop Sections: 5.4.1 Shared network infrastructure - VPC, subnets and NAT setup 5.4.10 Chat Service on ECS Fargate - Container deployment on ECS Fargate behind an ALB

title: 5.2.7 Cost Optimization and Clean-up
content:
Cost levers already in use Lambda for six of seven services — pay per invocation instead of an instance running all day; DEV traffic and the scheduled jobs largely fit in the Lambda free tier. Aurora Serverless v2 with a low floor — 0.5 ACU while services were being deployed (to avoid auto-pause noise in smoke tests), designed to go to 0 ACU when the environment is idle. One Aurora cluster with seven logical databases instead of seven clusters. OpenSearch Serverless NextGen at 0–2 OCU — scales to zero when idle instead of the default maximum of 96 OCU. Bedrock on demand — no model hosting cost; per-route throttling on the AI routes stops a client or frontend bug from generating runaway token usage. S3 static website for the frontend — near-zero cost for a build that never changes at request time. One NAT Gateway for the whole DEV VPC rather than one per Availability Zone. Right-sized Fargate task — 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB for the Chat Service; the migrator task (1 vCPU / 2 GB) only exists while it runs. Interface VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and OpenSearch keep that traffic off the NAT Gateway’s per-GB processing charge. Where the fixed cost is With almost everything usage-based, the hourly costs that run even when nobody uses the system are the NAT Gateway, the Chat ALB, the Fargate task, Aurora’s minimum capacity, the interface VPC endpoints and the public IPv4 addresses (NAT Elastic IP and the ALB’s addresses). The Proposal’s budget estimates them; they are the targets of the “sleep” strategy below.
Planned, not yet automated DEV sleep strategy — Aurora to 0 ACU, the Chat service to 0 tasks out of hours, and the NAT Gateway deleted between test sessions (see 5.7). CloudFront in front of a private frontend bucket, adding caching and HTTPS. AWS Budgets alert on the account so an unexpected charge is noticed within a day. Clean-up The full, dependency-ordered teardown of every resource in this architecture is in 5.7 Clean-up.

title: 5.4.7 Payment Service
content:
The Payment Service handles wallet top-ups, PT-contract payments, withdrawals and the provider webhooks. Its sensitive internal endpoints (checkout, wallet transfer, contract release, no-show, termination, gym withdrawals) are only reachable through direct Lambda invoke from Gym, User and AI — never through the public API.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_payment (11 Prisma migrations) Secret fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database Functions fitness-assistant-dev-payment, fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs, temporary fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migrate Provider PAYMENT_PROVIDER=VNPAY (MoMo, PayOS, ZaloPay supported by the code) With Payment’s database the Aurora cluster reaches this layout:
fitness-assistant-dev-aurora ├── fitness_assistant → Auth ├── fitness_assistant_user → User ├── fitness_assistant_fitness → Fitness ├── fitness_assistant_gym → Gym └── fitness_assistant_payment → Payment Step 1 — Secret and artifacts Create fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database (database = fitness_assistant_payment), then upload payment-migrate-lambda.zip (~69 MiB) and payment-lambda.zip to the deployments bucket.
Step 2 — Migration role fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migrate-role with the two managed policies and an inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migration-secret for fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database* only.
Step 3 — Migration Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-payment-migrate: 1024 MB, 15 minutes, handler dist/migrate-lambda.handler, DATABASE_SECRET_ID=fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database, both private app subnets and the Lambda SG, code from S3 in copy mode.
Step 4 — Run the 11 migrations Check that the secret really says database = fitness_assistant_payment, then invoke the function once with {}. The handler has a safety guard that only accepts this database name, creates the logical database if it is missing, and only runs prisma migrate deploy.
Expected result: database = fitness_assistant_payment, migrateExitCode = 0, 11 migrations found, All migrations have been successfully applied.
Step 5 — Runtime role fitness-assistant-dev-payment-lambda-role with the two managed policies plus:
fitness-assistant-dev-payment-database-secret for the Payment secret; fitness-assistant-dev-payment-service-invoke: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-user", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-gym" ] } ] } Step 6 — Payment Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-payment, 1024 MB, 30 s, handler dist/lambda.handler, code s3://fitness-assistant-deployments-dev-<account-id>/payment-lambda.zip, the same VPC as the other database Lambdas.
Variable Value NODE_ENV production DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/payment-database INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the shared value AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME / USER_LAMBDA_NAME / GYM_LAMBDA_NAME the three function names PAYMENT_PROVIDER VNPAY VNPAY_SIMULATE false FRONTEND_URL the S3 website endpoint PAYMENT_PUBLIC_URL the API Gateway invoke URL (used to build provider callback URLs) Provider credentials (VNPAY_TMN_CODE, VNPAY_HASH_SECRET, MoMo / PayOS / ZaloPay keys) are only added once a real sandbox credential exists.
Step 7 — API Gateway routes Create the Lambda integration fitness-assistant-dev-payment (payload 2.0). ANY /me and ANY /admin are already owned by other services, so Payment uses specific prefixes:
Group Routes Public payments and provider webhooks ANY /payments, ANY /payments/{proxy+} — covers GET /payments/webhook/vnpay, POST /payments/webhook/{provider}, GET /payments/vnpay/return User ANY /me/payments, /me/wallet, /me/pt-wallet, /me/withdrawals — each with its /{proxy+} route Admin ANY /admin/payments, ANY /admin/payments/{proxy+} /internal and /internal/{proxy+} are never created. Afterwards, open Integrations → Attach integrations to routes and confirm every Payment route points at fitness-assistant-dev-payment — a route without an integration returns Not Found.
Step 8 — Jobs Lambda and the reconciliation schedule fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs: same role, artifact, VPC and environment as the HTTP Lambda, handler dist/jobs-lambda.handler, 1024 MB, 1 minute.
Create fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs-scheduler-role (trust scheduler.amazonaws.com, inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-payment-jobs for the Payment jobs Lambda only), then the schedule fitness-assistant-dev-payment-reconciliation: rate(5 minutes), payload {"job": "reconciliation"}, enabled, 5 minutes / 2 retries, no DLQ, AWS-owned key.
Every 5 minutes the reconciliation job polls the gateway for pending confirmations, retries activations and refund cancellations, and cleans up stale transactions.
Step 9 — Wire Gym to Payment Gym was deployed before Payment existed, so it has to be told about it:
Add PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME=fitness-assistant-dev-payment to both fitness-assistant-dev-gym and fitness-assistant-dev-gym-jobs (payout and referral settlement also call Payment). No PAYMENT_SERVICE_URL is needed with direct invoke. Extend the Gym role’s invoke policy (or add fitness-assistant-dev-gym-invoke-payment): { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-user", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-payment" ] } The Gym scheduler role does not need this permission — the scheduler only invokes gym-jobs, and it is gym-jobs that calls Payment.
The payment loop is now closed:
Gym Lambda ──direct invoke──► Payment Lambda ──► Payment DB ──► Provider (VNPAY) │ webhook Gym Lambda ◄──callback── Payment Lambda ◄── API Gateway /payments ◄┘ The remaining work for this service is configuring at least one real sandbox provider (VNPAY first, since it is the code default) with its callback/webhook URLs, so checkout can be tested end to end.

title: 5.7 Clean-up
content:
The DEV environment is still in use for end-to-end testing, so this teardown has not been run yet. It lists every resource created in 5.4 in the order that avoids dependency errors. Deleting Aurora, the S3 buckets and the secrets is irreversible — export anything you want to keep first.
Every resource name starts with fitness-assistant-dev- (or fitness-assistant/dev/ for secrets), and everything lives in ap-southeast-1. Use Resource Groups & Tag Editor with that prefix to double-check nothing is left.
Pausing instead of deleting If the environment is only idle for a while, these steps remove most of the cost without losing anything:
Resource Pause action Effect Aurora Serverless v2 Set minimum capacity to 0 ACU (auto-pause) Compute cost stops while idle; storage is kept Chat ECS service Update service → desired tasks 0 No Fargate charge NAT Gateway Delete it and release its Elastic IP; recreate before the next test session Removes the largest fixed hourly cost; Lambdas lose outbound internet meanwhile OpenSearch Serverless Already scales to 0 OCU when idle (0–2 OCU group) No action needed Full teardown order EventBridge Scheduler — delete the 13 schedules (fitness-assistant-dev-user-*, -workout-*, -gym-*, -payment-reconciliation, -ai-*), then the 5 scheduler roles. API Gateway — delete the HTTP API fitness-assistant-dev-api (all routes, integrations, CORS and throttling settings go with it). Chat on ECS Update fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service to 0 tasks, then delete the service. Delete the ALB fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb, then the target group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg. Deregister and delete the task definitions fitness-assistant-dev-chat and fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator (all revisions). Delete the cluster fitness-assistant-dev-cluster. Lambda Remove the SQS trigger (event source mapping) from fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker — deleting a function does not delete its event source mappings. Delete all functions: auth, user, user-jobs, fitness, fitness-jobs, gym, gym-jobs, payment, payment-jobs, ai, ai-worker, ai-jobs, and the remaining *-migrate functions. SQS — delete fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks and fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq. OpenSearch Serverless — delete the collection fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors, its data access / network / encryption policies, the OpenSearch application and workspace, the OpenSearch VPC endpoint and the collection group fitness-assistant-dev-ai. Aurora — optionally take a final snapshot, disable deletion protection if it is on, delete the instance, then the cluster fitness-assistant-dev-aurora. Secrets Manager — delete every fitness-assistant/dev/* secret (database secrets, chat-database-url, internal-service-secret). Deletion is scheduled with a 7–30 day recovery window unless forced. ECR — delete fitness-assistant-dev-chat, fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator and the earlier fitness-assistant/* repositories from the container phase. S3 — empty, then delete: the frontend bucket, the uploads bucket, the deployments bucket and the data-migration bucket (versioned: delete all object versions too). CloudWatch Logs — delete /aws/lambda/fitness-assistant-dev-*, /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat and /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator. Network Delete the NAT Gateway fitness-assistant-dev-nat-a, wait until Deleted, then release its Elastic IP. Delete the interface VPC endpoints (Secrets Manager, OpenSearch). Delete the security groups: chat-alb-sg, chat-sg, vpce-sg, lambda-sg, aurora-sg (remove cross-references first). Delete the subnets, the route tables (public-rt, private-app-rt, private-db-rt), detach and delete the Internet Gateway, then delete fitness-assistant-dev-vpc. IAM — delete the fitness-assistant-dev-* roles (Lambda, ECS task/execution, migrator, scheduler) and their inline policies. Bedrock — nothing to delete (no provisioned resources); optionally cancel the Cohere Marketplace subscription. Verify Billing → Bills and Cost Explorer (filter by service, region ap-southeast-1) show no new charges for NAT Gateway, Aurora, Fargate, ALB, OpenSearch or public IPv4 addresses after the next day. Resource Groups & Tag Editor with the fitness-assistant-dev prefix returns nothing.

title: 5.4.8 AI Service — database, queue and Bedrock
content:
The AI Service is split into three Lambdas, each with a different timing requirement:
Function Handler Timeout Job fitness-assistant-dev-ai dist/lambda.handler 29–30 s HTTP API: chat, plans, marketplace, admin AI. Long generations are queued instead of run inline. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker dist/worker-lambda.handler 300 s Consumes the SQS queue and runs long workout/nutrition generations on Nova Pro. fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs dist/jobs-lambda.handler 600 s Scheduled jobs: personalized-service auto-accept and knowledge ingestion (PubMed, RSS, web, local evidence). Before deploying, the code was updated so that the AI Lambda verifies Bearer JWTs by invoking the Auth Lambda, calls Auth/User/Fitness/Payment by direct invoke, and its migration Lambda reads DATABASE_SECRET_ID and creates fitness_assistant_ai on its own.
Step 1 — Database secret Create fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database (database = fitness_assistant_ai). No CREATE DATABASE by hand: the migration Lambda connects to the postgres maintenance database, checks pg_database, creates fitness_assistant_ai if missing, then runs prisma migrate deploy, and refuses to run against any other database.
Step 2 — Migration role and Lambda Role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-migrate-role (two managed policies + inline fitness-assistant-dev-ai-migrate-secret allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database*).
Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-ai-migrate: Node.js 22.x, x86_64, 1024 MB, 5 minutes, handler dist/migrate-lambda.handler, artifact ai-migrate-lambda.zip (~21 MiB, direct upload), both private app subnets + Lambda SG, environment NODE_ENV=production, DATABASE_SECRET_ID=fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database, AI_DATABASE_NAME=fitness_assistant_ai.
Step 3 — Run the 22 migrations Test → Create new event with {} (or {"database": "fitness_assistant_ai"}), then invoke.
Expected result: status = ok, database = fitness_assistant_ai, databaseCreated = true, migrateExitCode = 0, 22 migrations found, All migrations have been successfully applied. The 22 migrations contain no DROP or TRUNCATE — only one de-duplication DELETE that does not affect a new database.
Step 4 — SQS queues SQS replaces Redis/BullMQ for AI plan generation in AWS.
SQS → Create queue, Standard, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq (defaults). Create queue, Standard, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks, visibility timeout 10 minutes (600 s) — longer than the Worker’s 300 s timeout, so a message is not redelivered while still being processed — with the dead-letter queue enabled: fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq, maximum receives 2. Copy the queue URL (https://sqs.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/<account-id>/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks) — it becomes AI_TASKS_QUEUE_URL.
Step 5 — Role for the AI HTTP Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role (AWS service → Lambda, two managed policies) with the inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-ai-runtime-policy:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:secret:fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database*" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sqs:SendMessage", "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-auth", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-user", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-fitness", "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-payment" ] } ] } Gym is not in the list because the AI code never calls it. The HTTP Lambda can only send to the queue; consuming is the Worker’s job.
Step 6 — Create the AI HTTP Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-ai: Node.js 22.x, x86_64, role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role, artifact ai-lambda.zip, handler dist/lambda.handler, 1024 MB, 30 s (later 29 s, just under API Gateway’s integration limit), private app subnets + Lambda SG.
The first environment still targeted the Anthropic API (LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic, called through the NAT Gateway because the endpoint is outside AWS):
Step 7 — Switch to Amazon Bedrock In Amazon Bedrock → Model catalog (region ap-southeast-1), both Amazon Nova Pro and Cohere Embed Multilingual were available. Decision: no Anthropic API key needed — the AI Service moved to Bedrock, which removes the external API key, keeps traffic on AWS and is billed through the same account. Cohere is a Marketplace model: accept its subscription/EULA once as an administrator (5.3.1).
Add these statements to fitness-assistant-dev-ai-runtime-policy (without removing the existing ones):
{ "Sid": "InvokeNovaProApacInferenceProfile", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock:InvokeModel", "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:inference-profile/apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0"] }, { "Sid": "InvokeNovaProOnlyThroughApacProfile", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock:InvokeModel", "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/amazon.nova-pro-v1:0"], "Condition": { "StringLike": { "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:inference-profile/apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0" } } }, { "Sid": "InvokeCohereEmbedMultilingualV3", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock:InvokeModel", "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1::foundation-model/cohere.embed-multilingual-v3"] } A cross-region inference profile can route to the foundation model in several APAC regions, so IAM must allow both the profile and the underlying foundation model — the condition limits the second statement to calls made through this profile. AmazonBedrockFullAccess and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream are not added; the code only uses InvokeModel.
Upload the new ai-lambda.zip built for Bedrock (35,076,525 bytes compressed, 105,103,760 bytes uncompressed — it bundles the Bedrock Runtime SDK and the Prisma rhel-openssl-3.0.x engine), keep the handler and VPC, and replace the environment with:
Variable Value NODE_ENV production DATABASE_SECRET_ID fitness-assistant/dev/ai-database INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET the shared value AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME, USER_LAMBDA_NAME, FITNESS_LAMBDA_NAME, PAYMENT_LAMBDA_NAME the four function names QUEUE_PROVIDER / AI_TASKS_QUEUE_URL sqs / the queue URL LLM_PROVIDER / BEDROCK_REGION bedrock / ap-southeast-1 BEDROCK_CHAT_MODEL / BEDROCK_VISION_MODEL apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 EMBEDDING_PROVIDER / BEDROCK_EMBEDDING_MODEL bedrock / cohere.embed-multilingual-v3 KNOWLEDGE_VECTOR_SIZE 1024 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS 25000 PLATFORM_COMMISSION_RATE / PERSONALIZED_SERVICE_AUTO_ACCEPT_DAYS 0.10 / 3 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, LLM_BASE_URL and OLLAMA_BASE_URL are removed. No migration is needed for the switch — the schema did not change.
The embedding dimension changed from 768 (Ollama, local development) to 1024 (Cohere). The code fails loudly if it is asked to write 1024-dimension vectors into an old 768-dimension index instead of corrupting it, so knowledge ingestion stays disabled until a 1024-dimension vector store exists — see 5.4.9.
Step 8 — AI Worker role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-role (“Execution role for Gymini AI Worker Lambda”), two managed policies, inline fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-runtime-policy with: the AI secret; sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:GetQueueAttributes on fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks; invoke on Auth/User/Fitness/Payment; and the same three Bedrock statements. Not added: AmazonBedrockFullAccess, AmazonSQSFullAccess, AWSLambdaFullAccess.
The resulting flow:
AI HTTP Lambda ──sqs:SendMessage──► fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks ──ReceiveMessage──► AI Worker Lambda ├── Nova Pro ├── Cohere Embed ├── Aurora └── internal Lambdas Step 9 — AI Worker Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker: Node.js 22.x, x86_64, role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-role, artifact ai-worker-lambda.zip (the new Bedrock build), handler dist/worker-lambda.handler (not dist/lambda.handler), 1024 MB, 300 s, ephemeral storage 512 MB, private app subnets only (never the DB subnets) + Lambda SG.
The Worker copies the HTTP Lambda’s environment with one important change: LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=180000 instead of 25000, because generations can run for minutes. AWS_REGION is not set manually (Lambda provides it), and no Anthropic/Ollama/Redis variables are needed.
Step 10 — SQS trigger for the Worker Check the queue first: visibility timeout 600 s, DLQ fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks-dlq, maximum receives 2.
Then Lambda → fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker → Add trigger → SQS: queue fitness-assistant-dev-ai-tasks, batch size 1, batch window 0, trigger activated, no filter, no maximum concurrency, and Report batch item failures enabled (the Worker returns batchItemFailures, so one failed message does not force the whole batch to retry).
Step 11 — AI Jobs role and Lambda Role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-role (two managed policies + inline fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-runtime-policy: the AI secret and the three Bedrock statements — Cohere for embeddings, Nova for LLM/safety judging).
Lambda fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs: artifact ai-lambda.zip, handler dist/jobs-lambda.handler, 1024 MB, 600 s (crawling plus embedding is long-running I/O and is not bound by API Gateway’s ~30 s limit), private app subnets + Lambda SG.
Environment: NODE_ENV, DATABASE_SECRET_ID, the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, LLM_PROVIDER=bedrock, BEDROCK_REGION, BEDROCK_CHAT_MODEL, BEDROCK_VISION_MODEL, EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=bedrock, BEDROCK_EMBEDDING_MODEL, KNOWLEDGE_VECTOR_SIZE=1024.
No schedule is attached yet: the knowledge jobs must not run until the 1024-dimension vector store exists. That is the next page.

title: 5.4.9 AI Service — vector search, scheduling and API
content:
The local development stack used Qdrant as the vector store. For AWS, the code was given a vector-store abstraction with an OpenSearch implementation (58/58 tests passing), so production no longer needs QDRANT_HOST / QDRANT_PORT. Requests to OpenSearch are signed with SigV4 (service aoss) using each Lambda’s IAM role — there is no OpenSearch username, password or API key.
Step 1 — Re-upload the three AI Lambdas The new build includes the OpenSearch client and SigV4 support (HTTP/Worker ZIP ≈ 36,325,814 bytes), so it is uploaded first, keeping each handler:
Function Artifact Handler fitness-assistant-dev-ai ai-lambda.zip dist/lambda.handler fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker ai-worker-lambda.zip dist/worker-lambda.handler fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs ai-lambda.zip dist/jobs-lambda.handler No database migration is required for this change.
Step 2 — Collection group with scale-to-zero Amazon OpenSearch Service → Serverless → Collection groups → Create collection group: generation NextGen, name fitness-assistant-dev-ai, description “Gymini AI vector search collection group”.
Capacity Min Max Indexing 0 OCU 2 OCU Search 0 OCU 2 OCU A minimum of 0 enables scale-to-zero: after about 10 idle minutes indexing and search drop to 0 OCU, and the first request after that can take an extra 10–30 seconds to wake up. A 0–2 OCU range is far more sensible for DEV than the default maximum of 96.
Step 3 — Private VPC endpoint OpenSearch Service → Serverless → VPC endpoints → Create VPC endpoint: VPC fitness-assistant-dev-vpc, subnets private-app-a and private-app-b. The runbook specifies the existing fitness-assistant-dev-vpce-sg (TCP 443 from the Lambda SG); the endpoint captured below (fitness-dev-opensearch-vpce) shows the Lambda SG attached — whichever group is attached must allow inbound TCP 443 from the Lambda security group. Wait for Available and note the endpoint ID (vpce-…, not the endpoint URL).
Step 4 — Vector search collection Serverless → Collections → Create collection: NextGen, Standard create (not Express — private networking and access policies must be controlled), name fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors, description “Gymini AI vector store for RAG and knowledge retrieval”, type Vector search, collection group fitness-assistant-dev-ai, AWS-owned encryption key.
Networking: access type Private, through the VPC endpoint above — no public access.
Data access: Create as a new data access policy named fitness-dev-ai-vector-access, defined as JSON rather than ticking permissions in the visual editor:
[ { "Description": "Fitness Assistant AI vector data access", "Rules": [ { "ResourceType": "collection", "Resource": ["collection/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors"], "Permission": ["aoss:DescribeCollectionItems"] }, { "ResourceType": "index", "Resource": ["index/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-vectors/*"], "Permission": [ "aoss:CreateIndex", "aoss:DescribeIndex", "aoss:UpdateIndex", "aoss:ReadDocument", "aoss:WriteDocument" ] } ], "Principal": [ "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role", "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-worker-role", "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-role" ] } ] aoss:DeleteIndex is deliberately not granted.
The wizard also creates an OpenSearch application (aoss-fitness-dev-ai) and workspace for browsing the data, with administrator permission limited to the account’s IAM principal.
When the collection is Active, copy its ARN (for IAM) and OpenSearch endpoint (https://<collection-id>.aoss.ap-southeast-1.on.aws, for the Lambdas) with the console’s copy buttons. Indexes are not created by hand.
Step 5 — IAM permission on all three AI roles The data access policy and IAM are two separate layers; missing either one returns 403. Add the inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-opensearch-access to each of fitness-assistant-dev-ai-lambda-role, -ai-worker-role and -ai-jobs-role:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccessAiVectorCollection", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "aoss:APIAccessAll", "Resource": "arn:aws:aoss:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:collection/<collection-id>" } ] } Not used: AmazonOpenSearchServerlessFullAccess, aoss:DashboardsAccessAll, aoss:* — the Lambdas only need the data-plane API.
Step 6 — Environment variables Add to all three AI Lambdas (and remove QDRANT_HOST / QDRANT_PORT if present):
VECTOR_STORE_PROVIDER=opensearch OPENSEARCH_REGION=ap-southeast-1 OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS_ENDPOINT=https://<collection-id>.aoss.ap-southeast-1.on.aws KNOWLEDGE_VECTOR_SIZE=1024 The Worker keeps LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=180000.
Amazon Bedrock / \ Nova Pro Cohere Embed (1024) │ ▼ OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) ▲ ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ AI HTTP AI Worker AI Jobs Step 7 — Let the code create the indexes The collection shows Indexes: - and stays that way: the indexes exercises, fitness_knowledge, fitness_faq and fitness_evidence are bootstrapped by the code on first use with the exact mapping it expects — vector field vector, type knn_vector, dimension 1024, engine faiss, method hnsw, space cosinesimil. If an index exists with the wrong dimension the code fails instead of deleting data.
Step 8 — Scheduler role for the AI jobs Custom trust policy for scheduler.amazonaws.com, role fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs-scheduler-role, inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-invoke-ai-jobs with lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-ai-jobs only.
Step 9 — Five schedules The auto-accept schedule: fitness-assistant-dev-ai-autoaccept, rate(15 minutes), payload {"job": "personalized-service-autoaccept-sweep"}, enabled, the AI jobs scheduler role.
Then four nightly knowledge-ingestion schedules (cron-based, time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh so they run at night Vietnam time):
Schedule Expression Payload fitness-assistant-dev-ai-local-evidence cron(0 2 * * ? *) {"job":"local-evidence-refresh"} fitness-assistant-dev-ai-pubmed cron(30 2 * * ? *) {"job":"pubmed-refresh"} fitness-assistant-dev-ai-rss cron(0 3 * * ? *) {"job":"rss-refresh"} fitness-assistant-dev-ai-web cron(30 3 * * ? *) {"job":"web-refresh"} EventBridge Scheduler → AI Jobs Lambda → PubMed / RSS / Web / Local → Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 (1024) → OpenSearch Serverless → fitness_knowledge / fitness_evidence … Step 10 — Connect the AI Lambda to API Gateway Create the Lambda integration fitness-assistant-dev-ai (payload 2.0) and eight routes:
ANY /ai ANY /ai/{proxy+} ANY /plans ANY /plans/{proxy+} ANY /marketplace ANY /marketplace/{proxy+} ANY /admin/ai ANY /admin/ai/{proxy+} The greedy routes cover POST /ai/ask, GET /ai/conversations, POST /ai/agent/goal-image, POST /plans/workout/generate, GET /plans/job/{id}, GET /admin/ai/overview and so on. Route authorization stays NONE: the AI Lambda verifies the Bearer JWT itself through the Auth Lambda and rejects spoofed x-user-id / x-user-role headers, so adding an API Gateway JWT authorizer would create a second, inconsistent auth layer. /internal/*, /metrics and /{proxy+} are not created.
Step 11 — Payment → AI After a successful payment, Payment activates the personalized service by invoking the AI Lambda’s internal endpoint POST /internal/personalized-service/orders/:id/activate-after-payment (idempotent, so retries are safe). Add AI_LAMBDA_NAME=fitness-assistant-dev-ai to both fitness-assistant-dev-payment and fitness-assistant-dev-payment-jobs, and add to the Payment role:
{ "Sid": "InvokeAiService", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction", "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:function:fitness-assistant-dev-ai" } No public URL, /internal route or Lambda Function URL is created for this. The chain is now: user → AI marketplace → Payment → provider → webhook/reconciliation → Payment Lambda → (direct invoke) AI Lambda → activate service.
Step 12 — Rate-limit the AI routes to protect Bedrock cost The old application gateway limited /ai/ask to 20 requests per 60 seconds, and the AI Service has no per-user token budget, so without a limit a frontend bug could send hundreds of billable Bedrock calls. In API Gateway → fitness-assistant-dev-api → Stages → $default → route throttling, limit only the AI routes (not the whole API):
Route Rate (req/s) Burst ANY /ai, ANY /ai/{proxy+} 1 3 ANY /plans, ANY /plans/{proxy+} 1 3 ANY /marketplace, ANY /marketplace/{proxy+} 3 6 ANY /admin/ai, ANY /admin/ai/{proxy+} 1 3 API Gateway uses a token bucket and returns HTTP 429 when the limit is exceeded; the limits are best-effort targets, not hard ceilings, and they apply per route, not per user. The frontend must show a “too many requests, try again later” message with backoff instead of retrying in a loop. Usage plans / API keys (a REST API feature) and Lambda reserved concurrency (which would throttle all AI routes together) are deliberately not used.
The full AI path now has: JWT → API Gateway route throttling → AI HTTP Lambda (Auth, Aurora, Nova Pro, Cohere, OpenSearch, SQS) → AI Worker; EventBridge → AI Jobs → OpenSearch; Payment → AI internal endpoint.

Free Tier vs. promotional credit vs. pay-as-you-go: three different things, and having credit does not mean the infrastructure is free — it only postpones real billing. Fixed-cost vs. usage-based resources: most of this project’s services bill by usage, but a few (NAT Gateway, Aurora’s capacity floor, the Chat Fargate task, the ALB, VPC endpoints, public IPv4) bill by the hour regardless of traffic, which is exactly the resource profile already estimated in the Proposal’s budget. AWS CloudFormation: stacks, templates, parameters, outputs, Change Sets, drift detection, and — importantly — what it does not guarantee (cost reduction, or that deleting a stack removes every resource). Technical Writing: structuring a case study that separates confirmed facts from reasonable inference, instead of presenting everything as equally certain. Hands-on Labs Completed:

Writing this case study turned into an honest audit of the project’s own operational gaps:

title: 5.4.10 Chat Service on ECS Fargate
content:
Chat is the only service that does not run on Lambda: Socket.IO keeps a connection open for the whole chat session, which does not fit Lambda’s per-invocation model. It runs as one container on ECS Fargate, behind its own Application Load Balancer.
Item Value Logical database fitness_assistant_chat (3 Prisma migrations) Secrets fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database (migration), fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database-url (runtime), fitness-assistant/dev/internal-service-secret Image ECR fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 Runtime Cluster fitness-assistant-dev-cluster, service fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service, task definition fitness-assistant-dev-chat — 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, container port 3005 Entry points Socket.IO → ALB fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb (HTTP 80); REST → API Gateway ANY /chat/{proxy+} → ALB Internet ─:80─► chat-alb-sg ─:3005─► chat-sg (Fargate task, private subnets) ─:5432─► aurora-sg Part A — Database Step 1 — Database secret. Secrets Manager → Other type of secret → Plaintext, reusing the username/password/host/port of a working database secret and changing only the database name:
{ "username": "<Aurora username>", "password": "<Aurora password>", "host": "fitness-assistant-dev-aurora.cluster-<id>.ap-southeast-1.rds.amazonaws.com", "port": 5432, "database": "fitness_assistant_chat" } Name fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database, description “Chat Service Aurora PostgreSQL database – dev”, default aws/secretsmanager key, rotation off. The secret only stores connection details — the database itself is created by the migration Lambda.
Step 2 — Migration role. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate-role (“Execution role for Chat Service database migration Lambda”) with AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole + AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole and the inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate-secret (secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database* only). No Bedrock, SQS, OpenSearch or invoke permissions — the migration needs only logs, VPC access and its secret.
Step 3 — Migration Lambda. At this point the account already ran 15 functions:
Create fitness-assistant-dev-chat-migrate (Node.js 22.x, x86_64, role above), upload backend/services/chat-service/artifacts/chat-migrate-lambda.zip, handler dist/migrate-lambda.handler, 1024 MB, 1 minute, DATABASE_SECRET_ID=fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database, both private app subnets + Lambda SG.
Step 4 — Run the migration. Test event chat-migrate with {}. Expected: status: ok, database: fitness_assistant_chat, databaseCreated: true (false if it already existed), migrateExitCode: 0, 3 migrations applied. If it fails, record the error instead of re-running it repeatedly.
Part B — Container image Step 5 — ECR repository. ECR → Create repository: private, name fitness-assistant-dev-chat, tag mutability Mutable (tags are reused during DEV; production should use commit-based tags such as git-a84f23c), AES-256 encryption, scan on push if offered.
Step 6 — Push the image from PowerShell on the workstation. Build only if the image is missing:
docker images gymini-chat-service # only if missing: docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t gymini-chat-service:aws-local -f backend/services/chat-service/Dockerfile . aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-southeast-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com docker tag gymini-chat-service:aws-local <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 Login Succeeded must appear before tagging; 'aws' is not recognized, Unable to locate credentials or AccessDeniedException mean stopping to fix the CLI setup first.
Part C — Logs and IAM Step 7 — Log group. CloudWatch → Create log group /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat (ECS convention, not /aws/lambda/...), retention 30 days.
Step 8 — Task execution role (used by ECS itself to pull the image, write logs and inject secrets — not by the application). Trusted entity Elastic Container Service → Elastic Container Service Task, managed policy AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy, name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-role, plus an inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-secrets allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the Chat secrets.
Step 9 — Task role (what the Chat code uses at runtime). Same trusted entity, no managed policy, name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-task-role, inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service-invoke allowing lambda:InvokeFunction on fitness-assistant-dev-auth and fitness-assistant-dev-user only. No Secrets Manager permissions here — secrets are injected by the execution role.
Part D — Network Step 10 — Security group for the task. EC2 → Security Groups → Create: fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg (“Security group for Chat Service Fargate tasks”), no inbound rule yet, default outbound (the task calls the Auth/User Lambdas, Aurora and DNS).
Step 11 — Let the task reach Aurora. RDS → fitness-assistant-dev-aurora → Connectivity & security → open the Aurora security group → Edit inbound rules → PostgreSQL 5432 from security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg (“Allow Chat Fargate tasks to Aurora”). Never 0.0.0.0/0 on 5432.
Step 12 — ECS cluster. ECS → Clusters → Create cluster: fitness-assistant-dev-cluster, infrastructure Fargate only, no EC2 capacity, no Service Connect.
Part E — Runtime secrets and task definition Step 13 — Runtime secrets. The Chat code reads CHAT_DATABASE_URL, not DATABASE_URL. Create fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database-url holding postgresql://USERNAME:PASSWORD@<aurora-endpoint>:5432/fitness_assistant_chat?schema=public (URL-encode special characters in the password, e.g. @ → %40), stored under the JSON key CHAT_DATABASE_URL. Reuse the shared internal secret as fitness-assistant/dev/internal-service-secret (same value the Lambdas use, never a new one). Extend the execution role policy to both secrets.
Step 14 — Task definition. ECS → Task definitions → Create new task definition:
Setting Value Family fitness-assistant-dev-chat Launch type / OS AWS Fargate, Linux/X86_64, network mode awsvpc Task size 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB Task role / execution role fitness-assistant-dev-chat-task-role / fitness-assistant-dev-chat-execution-role Container chat-service, essential, image …/fitness-assistant-dev-chat:dev-20260922-1 Port mapping 3005/TCP, app protocol HTTP, name chat-http Environment NODE_ENV=production, CHAT_SERVICE_PORT=3005, CORS_ORIGIN=<S3 website URL>, ENABLE_REST_CORS=true, AUTH_LAMBDA_NAME, USER_LAMBDA_NAME Secrets (ValueFrom) CHAT_DATABASE_URL ← <chat-database-url secret ARN>:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::; INTERNAL_API_SECRET (alias INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET) ← internal-service-secret Logging awslogs, group /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat, region ap-southeast-1, stream prefix chat Health check none in the task; the ALB checks /health (the image may not contain curl/wget) Lesson learned. In revision 1 the secret entries were typed with value type Value, so the container received the secret name instead of the connection string and Prisma failed with URL must start with postgresql://. The fix was a new revision whose secrets use ValueFrom with the full secret ARN plus the JSON key suffix (…:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::), then Update service → revision 3 → Force new deployment. Never paste the real values into plain environment variables.
Part F — Load balancer Step 15 — ALB security group. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg (“ALB security group for Fitness Assistant Chat dev”): inbound HTTP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 (the frontend itself is still HTTP; HTTPS 443 comes with a domain and ACM certificate).
Step 16 — Only the ALB may reach the task. In fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg add Custom TCP 3005 with source = security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg (“Allow Chat ALB to reach ECS task”). Port 3005 is never opened to 0.0.0.0/0.
Step 17 — Second public subnet. An internet-facing ALB needs two Availability Zones, so fitness-assistant-dev-public-b (10.0.2.0/24, ap-southeast-1b) was added — see 5.4.1, step 6.
Step 18 — Target group. EC2 → Target groups → Create: target type IP addresses (Fargate uses awsvpc, so not Instances), name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg, HTTP 3005, IPv4, HTTP1; health check /health, healthy 2, unhealthy 3, timeout 5 s, interval 20 s, success code 200. Register no targets — the ECS service registers task IPs itself. Then set deregistration delay 30 s and stickiness (load-balancer cookie, 1 day), which suits Socket.IO’s polling fallback.
Step 19 — Application Load Balancer. fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb, internet-facing, IPv4, subnets public-a and public-b, security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-sg only, listener HTTP:80 → forward to fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg. Record the DNS name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb-<id>.ap-southeast-1.elb.amazonaws.com.
Step 20 — Idle timeout 120 s. ALB → Attributes → idle timeout from 60 to 120 seconds, better suited to long-lived WebSocket connections.
Step 21 — Hide internal paths. The default listener action forwards every path, including /internal/* and /metrics. Add two rules to HTTP:80: priority 1, path /internal/* → fixed response 404 text/plain “Not Found”; priority 2, path /metrics → the same. /health, /chat/* and /socket.io/* still reach the container.
Part G — Service Step 22 — ECS service. Cluster → Services → Create:
Setting Value Compute Launch type FARGATE, platform LATEST Task definition fitness-assistant-dev-chat (latest revision) Service name fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service, replica, 1 desired task Networking private-app-a + private-app-b only, security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg, public IP off Load balancing existing ALB fitness-assistant-dev-chat-alb, container chat-service 3005:3005, existing listener HTTP:80, existing target group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-tg Health check grace period 60 s Service Connect / discovery / auto scaling off Desired count stays 1: Socket.IO session state is kept in memory, so a second task would split sessions until a shared adapter (e.g. Redis) is added.
Right after creation the service shows Running 0 / Pending 1 while it pulls the image, injects secrets and creates the ENI. If a task stops, read Stopped reason and the service Events instead of recreating the service.
Step 23 — Verify. The service runs 1/1 tasks and the target group reports one Healthy private IP on port 3005.
Then http://<alb-dns>/health, and the Socket.IO handshake http://<alb-dns>/socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=polling, which must answer 0{"sid":"…","upgrades":["websocket"],…} — not 404, 502 or 503. See 5.5.3.
Part H — Wire it into the API and the frontend Step 24 — REST through API Gateway. In fitness-assistant-dev-api create route ANY /chat/{proxy+} with an HTTP URI integration: method ANY, URL http://<alb-dns>/chat/{proxy}. The {proxy} part matters — /chat/conversations must reach the backend as /chat/conversations. Test with GET https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/chat/conversations (a Bearer token is needed for real data).
Step 25 — Frontend. Set the Socket.IO URL (VITE_CHAT_WS_URL) to the ALB, rebuild and republish with the redeploy procedure:
REST: Frontend → API Gateway → /chat/{proxy+} → Chat ALB → ECS Socket.IO: Frontend → Chat ALB → /socket.io/ → ECS Step 26 — Roll out the fixed task definition. ECS → fitness-assistant-dev-cluster → fitness-assistant-dev-chat-service → Update → task definition fitness-assistant-dev-chat:3, everything else unchanged, Force new deployment. Target state: 1 running, 0 pending, deployment Completed, and no more URL must start with postgresql:// in /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-chat.

title: 5.4.11 Data migration to Aurora
content:
The schemas on Aurora were created by each service’s migration Lambda. This last step moved the data of the 7 local PostgreSQL databases into them — keeping the original IDs, without reseeding — using a one-shot ECS Fargate task that runs pg_restore inside the VPC.
The order was fixed in advance so nothing could be corrupted halfway:
Upload the 7 dumps and their manifest to a private S3 bucket. Make sure all 7 logical databases exist on Aurora (including fitness_assistant_chat). Apply the latest schema migrations to all 7. Build and push a migrator image to ECR. Run a read-only preflight task. Restore every database. Compare row counts / primary keys. Only then handle uploaded files and vector data. Step 1 — Private migration bucket S3 → Create bucket fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id> in ap-southeast-1: Block all public access on, versioning enabled, SSE-S3 encryption, no static website. A dedicated bucket keeps dumps away from the public frontend bucket and the user-uploads bucket.
Create the prefixes full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps/, manifests/ and user-files/.
Step 2 — Upload the dumps and the manifest Upload the 7 audited dumps unchanged (not unzipped, not converted to SQL): gymcoach_auth, _user, _fitness, _gym, _payment, _chat and _ai .data.dump — 72.9 MB in total — then the SHA-256 manifest.json to manifests/.
Never upload .env, .env.production, database passwords, JWT_SECRET, INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, AWS credentials or provider API keys to this bucket.
Step 3 — Migrator image A minimal image with only pg_restore and the AWS CLI, reusable for all 7 databases (and later for CI/CD). Create the ECR repository fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator (private, mutable, AES-256).
tools/db-migrator/Dockerfile:
FROM postgres:16-bookworm RUN apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends awscli ca-certificates \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /work ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/bash", "-lc"] CMD ["echo 'db-migrator ready'"] docker build -t fitness-assistant-db-migrator:dev . docker run --rm fitness-assistant-db-migrator:dev "pg_restore --version && aws --version" # pg_restore 16.15, aws-cli 2.9.19 aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-southeast-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com docker tag fitness-assistant-db-migrator:dev <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:dev-20260923-1 docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:dev-20260923-1 Step 4 — Roles Execution role fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-execution-role (ECS task, AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy) — pulls the image and writes logs.
Task role fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-task-role with the inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-runtime — read the dumps prefix only, and read the Aurora credential:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadMigrationDumps", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id>/full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps/*"] }, { "Sid": "ListMigrationDumpPrefix", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketLocation"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id>"], "Condition": { "StringLike": { "s3:prefix": ["full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps/*"] } } }, { "Sid": "ReadAuroraCredential", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:secret:fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database-*"] } ] } Step 5 — Task definition ECS → Create new task definition fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator: Fargate, Linux/X86_64, awsvpc, 1 vCPU / 2 GB, the two roles, container db-migrator with image …/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:dev-20260923-1, no port mapping needed, environment AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1, DB_SECRET_ID=fitness-assistant/dev/chat-database, DUMP_S3_PREFIX=s3://fitness-assistant-data-migration-dev-<account-id>/full-local-migration/2026-09/dumps, logs to /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator, default ephemeral storage (far more than the 73 MB of dumps). No command is set — it is overridden at run time.
Step 6 — Inject the database URL as a secret (revision 2) Give the execution role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the chat-database-url secret (inline policy fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator-secret), then create revision 2 with a secret environment variable DATABASE_URL, value type ValueFrom, value <chat-database-url secret ARN>:CHAT_DATABASE_URL::. DB_SECRET_ID is no longer needed.
The script derives the server URL from DATABASE_URL and switches the database name per restore, so one credential serves all 7 logical databases on the same cluster.
Step 7 — Preflight (read-only) ECS → fitness-assistant-dev-cluster → Tasks → Run new task: FARGATE, fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:2, 1 task, private app subnets, security group fitness-assistant-dev-chat-sg (already allowed into Aurora on 5432 and into the Secrets Manager endpoint), public IP disabled, no load balancer. Command override for db-migrator:
set -euo pipefail; echo "=== DB MIGRATOR PREFLIGHT START ==="; echo "Region=$AWS_REGION"; echo "Prefix=$DUMP_S3_PREFIX"; test -n "${DATABASE_URL:-}"; PSQL_URL="${DATABASE_URL%%\?*}"; mkdir -p /work/dumps; aws s3 ls "$DUMP_S3_PREFIX/"; aws s3 cp "$DUMP_S3_PREFIX/" /work/dumps/ --recursive --only-show-errors; ls -lh /work/dumps; for f in gymcoach_auth.data.dump gymcoach_user.data.dump gymcoach_fitness.data.dump gymcoach_gym.data.dump gymcoach_payment.data.dump gymcoach_chat.data.dump gymcoach_ai.data.dump; do test -s "/work/dumps/$f"; pg_restore -l "/work/dumps/$f" >/dev/null; echo "OK dump: $f"; done; echo "Checking Aurora databases..."; psql "$PSQL_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -Atc "select datname from pg_database where datname in ('fitness_assistant','fitness_assistant_user','fitness_assistant_fitness','fitness_assistant_gym','fitness_assistant_payment','fitness_assistant_chat','fitness_assistant_ai') order by datname;"; echo "=== DB MIGRATOR PREFLIGHT OK ===" Expected result at the end of /ecs/fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator: === DB MIGRATOR PREFLIGHT OK === — every dump downloads and is readable by pg_restore -l, and all 7 databases exist. If the task stops with an error, record the stopped reason and last log lines before going further.
Step 8 — Restore Destructive DEV operation. This step empties every table (except _prisma_migrations) in the 7 Aurora DEV databases and replaces the data with the local dumps. The schema and migration history are not touched. Run it only after the preflight succeeded.
Same run-task settings, with this command override:
set -euo pipefail; echo "=== FULL RESTORE START ==="; mkdir -p /work/dumps; aws s3 cp "$DUMP_S3_PREFIX/" /work/dumps/ --recursive --only-show-errors; PSQL_URL="${DATABASE_URL%%\?*}"; BASE="${PSQL_URL%/*}"; restore_db(){ DB="$1"; DUMP="$2"; URL="$BASE/$DB"; echo "=== CLEAN $DB ==="; T=$(psql "$URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -Atc "select string_agg(format('%I.%I', schemaname, tablename), ',') from pg_tables where schemaname='public' and tablename <> '_prisma_migrations';"); if [ -n "$T" ]; then psql "$URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c "TRUNCATE TABLE $T RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;"; fi; echo "=== RESTORE $DB FROM $DUMP ==="; pg_restore --exit-on-error --no-owner --no-privileges --data-only --exclude-table-data=public._prisma_migrations --dbname="$URL" "/work/dumps/$DUMP"; echo "=== DONE $DB ==="; }; restore_db fitness_assistant gymcoach_auth.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_user gymcoach_user.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_fitness gymcoach_fitness.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_gym gymcoach_gym.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_payment gymcoach_payment.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_chat gymcoach_chat.data.dump; restore_db fitness_assistant_ai gymcoach_ai.data.dump; echo "=== FULL RESTORE OK ===" Expected result: === DONE fitness_assistant_ai === followed by === FULL RESTORE OK ===.
Step 9 — Handle schema drift with a scripted migrator The local dumps and the Aurora schemas were not guaranteed to be identical — for example the Gym data could use brand_id where the Aurora schema still had gym_id, which would make the restore fail or require a deliberate patch. The one-line command was therefore replaced by a script inside the image, selected with a MODE variable, and the task definition went through further revisions (up to fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:11). From PowerShell:
$CLUSTER = "fitness-assistant-dev-cluster" $TASKDEF = "fitness-assistant-dev-db-migrator:11" $REGION = "ap-southeast-1" $NET = "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[<private-app-a-id>,<private-app-b-id>],securityGroups=[<chat-sg-id>],assignPublicIp=DISABLED}" aws ecs run-task ` --cluster $CLUSTER ` --task-definition $TASKDEF ` --launch-type FARGATE ` --network-configuration $NET ` --region $REGION ` --overrides '{\"containerOverrides\":[{\"name\":\"db-migrator\",\"environment\":[{\"name\":\"MODE\",\"value\":\"apply-prepatch\"}]}]}' MODE=apply-prepatch applies the schema pre-patches; the log must show schema-prepatch applied and the task must stop with exit code 0. Review the generated db-migrator-output/generated/needs-review.fitness_assistant_gym.sql in the migration bucket and decide the gym_id → brand_id case deliberately. Run MODE=restore. Result According to the deployment status table, all 7 of 7 service databases were restored and 23 of 23 audited foreign keys were applied and validated. Uploaded user files (user-files/) and re-embedding the local Qdrant data into OpenSearch are separate follow-ups, done only after the relational data was verified.
